content: Anthropic said on Sunday that it would set aside large portions of its wealth to support initiatives it believes are in the public interest. In a blog post, the AI colossus said it aims to establish a separate LLC that would use Anthropic shares to make donations to nonprofits or "direct distributions to specific populations." The new LLC, called the "Anthropic Public Benefit Fund," would receive larger stakes as the company grows. The company said an initial funding round of 5% of Anthropic's shares is still subject to stockholder approval. "The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways," the company said. A 5% stake in Anthropic is worth about $48 billion, according to the company's most recent valuation in May. In 2025, rival frontier AI company OpenAI established a similar nonprofit foundation with a multibillion-dollar stake in the company to fund public-benefit initiatives. Author of the AI Insider newsletter AI companies have already scraped much of the web. Now they're chasing something even more valuable: data that shows how humans actually work. That's the focus of Business Insider's new series, The AI Data Grab. This week, we published three stories showing how the race for workplace data is accelerating. One piece, from Charles Rollet, Tom Carter, and Stephen Council, examines the booming market for company records. AI firms are offering businesses six- and even seven-figure sums for anonymized Slack messages, emails, presentations, and internal documents. The goal is to teach AI systems how people solve problems, collaborate, make decisions, and complete long, multi-step tasks. Those real-world workflows are becoming the fuel for the next generation of AI agents. Another story, from Melia Robinson, explores how law firms are building AI systems around decades of legal knowledge, turning their own experience into a competitive advantage rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf AI models and tools. A third piece, by Rya Jetha, reveals how AI companies pay people to record real-world work, such as cooking dinners and packing warehouses, to teach robots how humans perform everyday physical tasks. Together, these stories point to a major shift in AI development. The first wave of generative AI was mostly about bigger models and faster chips. The next chapter is about machines understanding how work gets done, so AI can help us do it better and quicker. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Berkshire Hathaway's latest bet isn't a no-brainer or a head-scratcher; it's somewhere in between. Berkshire — which has seen Warren Buffett retire as CEO and chairman since the turn of the year — has agreed to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, on top of a $600 million injection when the Italian tech conglomerate went public in July, giving the Nebraska behemoth a 4% stake. Bending Spoons disclosed Berkshire's backing in a press release on Wednesday, catapulting its stock up nearly 50% over two days, a phenomenon known as the "Buffett effect." The stock fell on Friday, but still ended the week more than 20% above Monday's opening price. Berkshire has agreed to buy 10 million shares for $33 each, around a 13% discount to Bending Spoons' closing price of $38 on Tuesday, the day before the deal was announced. CEO and cofounder Luca Ferrari described Berkshire in the press release as "among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world," and a "longstanding inspiration" for Bending Spoons. Neither company responded to requests for comment from Business Insider. Bending Spoons acquires digital businesses, transforms and optimizes them to increase profits, then reinvests those earnings in further acquisitions. It has been pursuing that strategy for more than a decade and has never sold a material business. Its acquisitions to date include AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite, and WeTransfer. Ferrari's company said in the press release that it "strives to envision the most successful version of an acquired business," then works to close the gap between that vision and reality "as quickly and completely as possible." Bending Spoons said that typically involves "deep" transformation such as "reorganizing teams, overhauling technology, redesigning user interfaces, accelerating product development, and enhancing marketing and monetization," often with a good dose of AI. Ferrari gave the example of Evernote on a recent episode of the "Joys of Compounding" podcast. He said the business had around 350 employees when Bending Spoons acquired it at the start of 2023. That shrank to roughly 60 within 12 to 18 months, and now it's being run by around 20 people. Yet Ferrari said Evernote "launched by far the biggest update to the product in maybe a decade" this spring. First and foremost, Bending Spoons is a tech conglomerate, and Berkshire has eschewed tech for most of its history with a few big exceptions, namely Apple and Alphabet. That's because Buffett is a bargain hunter who likes to invest with a "margin of safety" in case something goes wrong, and tries to stay within his "circle of competence," only buying into what he deeply understands. Tech companies have rarely been a good fit for his approach, as they typically have lofty valuations, unpredictable outlooks, and complex products and services. Indeed, Bending Spoons generated 32 cents in earnings per share last year. Berkshire is paying more than 100 times that per share in the coming private placement. It's true that Bending Spoons is growing fast, with revenue surging 126% year-on-year to $704 million in the second quarter and adjusted operating income jumping 150% to $381 million. Few, however, would consider the stock a bargain from a fundamental perspective. Berkshire is also famously a hands-off acquirer, offering founders the opportunity to cash out while continuing to run their businesses as they see fit. In contrast, a core aspect of Bending Spoons' strategy is revamping its acquisitions. Berkshire and Bending Spoons have similarities as well as differences. Both are decentralized conglomerates that buy businesses not to flip them, but to own them for the long term. Berkshire is a web of largely autonomous companies, including GEICO, Duracell, Fruit of the Loom, Pilot Travel Centers, and BNSF Railway. It has long offered a permanent home to the businesses it buys. Bending Spoons has positioned itself as a forever owner, too, emulating Berkshire's approach of taking the cash generated by a subsidiary like See's Candies and using it to acquire more businesses. Ferrari said in his recent podcast interview that Bending Spoons has fostered a culture of caring deeply about the company, and doesn't centralize decision-making in part because that "deprives people of that precious sense of ownership." Buffett famously wrote "An Owner's Manual" for Berkshire shareholders. He's championed that mindset by keeping more than 99% of his net worth in Berkshire stock, and encouraging the company's other executives and directors to have skin in the game too. Ferrari also said on the podcast that he has a "pathological love of learning" across different domains. That echoes Buffett's boundless curiosity and the late Charlie Munger's insatiable appetite for knowledge. Buffett's longtime business partner studied architecture, physics, history, meteorology, psychology, law, and, of course, investing, among other subjects. Beyond their similar philosophies, it's worth noting that investing less than $1 billion into Bending Spoons isn't a huge deal for Berkshire. It has a $1.1 trillion market capitalization, had a $365 billion cash pile at the end of June, and its biggest stock position was worth about $66 billion at that time. The Bending Spoons deal could mark an evolution in Berkshire's investing style following Buffett's departure as CEO and chairman. Berkshire hasn't commented on the purchase or on whether Buffett was involved. Its relatively small size could mean his remaining investment manager, Ted Weschler, was behind it. Or it might be new CEO Greg Abel, who piled an additional $10 billion into Alphabet in a private placement this summer after consulting with Buffett. Whoever was responsible, and whatever their reasons for investing, this will be an intriguing wager to watch for Berkshire followers. No comments right now, check back later. A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe, bringing a new twist to the bombastic short-seller's fraud conviction. Left's lawyers this month asked the judge who oversaw his trial to toss the jury's verdict convicting him of 13 counts of securities fraud. The trial was irredeemably unfair, they said, because they never had the chance to ask the witness about the investigation and attack his credibility. "A new trial would probably produce an acquittal," Left's lawyers wrote. In June, a federal jury in Los Angeles found Left guilty of 13 counts of securities fraud. Prosecutors said he deceived investors by using social media and research reports to set target prices for stocks — including Tesla, Nvidia, and Palantir — while quietly trading them at different prices with his own money. The founder of Citron Research, Left is something of a short-seller celebrity. He placed bets against GameStop at the same time it became a meme stock, which pitted him against some retail traders on social media. For years, he was a fixture on CNBC and Bloomberg, where he shared his views on stock prices. Left hasn't been sentenced. In addition to the criminal case, he faces a parallel civil lawsuit from the Securities and Exchange Commission that remains unresolved. Left's criminal conviction shook certain corners of Wall Street, which viewed the trial as a referendum on free speech and the legality of activist short-seller tactics. Left, testifying in his own defense at the trial, said that the views he shared about public companies were sincere. One of the trial's prosecution witnesses was Daniel Bachus, the CFO of Grand Canyon Education, a publicly traded technology company that provides services to universities. Left's lawyers say that Bachus was the only witness who testified that Left used his Citron Research reports to lie about a company, not merely omit information. On August 21 — weeks after the trial ended — Grand Canyon Education placed Bachus on paid administrative leave "in connection with an ongoing governmental investigation" involving a non-employee's trades of the company's stock, the company said in an SEC disclosure. The prosecutors in Left's case referred to it in their own filings as an "insider trading investigation." No government agency has publicly accused Bachus or Grand Canyon Education of any misconduct in connection with the investigation. In the SEC disclosure, the company said it wasn't the focus of the investigation. Representatives for the SEC and for Grand Canyon Education declined to comment. Bachus didn't respond to Business Insider's requests for comment. Left's lawyers say they should have been informed about the investigation at the time of the trial so that they could cross-examine Bachus and try to convince the jury that he wasn't a credible witness. "This evidence would have destroyed the credibility of the government's only false-statements witness," they wrote in a filing. The prosecution team told Left's lawyers it didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. It's not clear which government agency opened the investigation, nor when Bachus or Grand Canyon Education became aware of it. Many of the filings about the issue remained sealed or redacted on the court docket for Left's case. In court filings, Justice Department prosecutors said Left's lawyers overstated Bachus' role in the short-selling case, which alleged securities fraud involving more than a dozen different public companies. They said Left wanted to conduct "his own shadow investigation into Bachus" to try to discredit him as a witness. "The law does not permit fishing expeditions in search of a claim," prosecutors said. Left declined to comment. Left's attorney Eric S. Rosen said he could not comment because many relevant documents remained under seal. A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in Los Angeles declined to comment. No comments right now, check back later. Comments are unavailable right now. Jump to

ReadWrite's editorial staff consists of journalists, editors, and experts across iGaming & Technology. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… Prediction-market operators cannot advertise through Google Ads to residents of Connecticut, Michigan, Nevada, New York or Ohio, as disputes over sports-related event contracts continue in state and federal courts. CDC Gaming reported that the restriction affects Kalshi and other operators. The five-state list creates an advertising barrier even as the underlying legal questions remain unsettled. Google’s policy sets conditions for where these companies can advertise, separate from the cases over whether states can stop them from offering contracts. Google added a section on prediction markets to its main Google Ads policies document in the week before CDC Gaming published its report. The rules cover platforms that list, or provide customers access to, exchange-listed contracts tied to economics, sports or current events. To advertise in an eligible location, a provider must hold the applicable local financial, commodities or gaming licences, comply with local laws and Google’s ad policies, and receive Google’s certification and approval. The company also requires advertisers to check the rules in each location they target. Those conditions apply alongside the state exclusions: Connecticut, Michigan, Nevada, New York and Ohio. CDC Gaming reported that sports-event contracts are not available in Michigan or Nevada, a distinction from the wider advertising restriction, which covers prediction-market products. CDC Gaming said each of the five states has sued prediction-market operators in an effort to block them from operating within its jurisdiction. Connecticut’s action against Kalshi is one example of the conflict over whether sports contracts fall under federal commodities regulation or state gambling rules, a dispute also reflected in Connecticut’s challenge to Kalshi’s sports contracts. Operators have also challenged state enforcement. Underdog sued Tennessee, its attorney general and the Tennessee Sports Wagering Council after receiving a cease-and-desist order over sports-event contracts. The company said Tennessee had warned it could face fines, civil penalties, criminal investigations and the loss of its fantasy sports operator licence if it did not comply. In its filing, Underdog asked a federal court in Nashville to prevent Tennessee from barring the contracts. The company’s position is that the CFTC regulates its event contracts and that federal oversight exempts them from the state’s gambling laws. Underdog has sued seven states over efforts to stop its sports-event contracts: Washington, Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Mexico, Ohio, Wisconsin and Tennessee. The arguments remain claims by the company, not a resolution of the broader regulatory dispute. The competing approaches to federal and state oversight of prediction markets have left operators facing both legal challenges and location-specific advertising limits. Google’s restrictions do not decide whether a state can regulate a contract; they determine where an eligible provider can buy ads through the platform. Sports outcomes are also the most common category among prediction-market users, according to the S&P Global Market Intelligence Kagan Q3 2026 Consumer Insights survey reported by CDC Gaming. Of respondents who used a yes-or-no exchange in the past year, 70% traded sports-event contracts, compared with 36% who traded economic or financial outcomes and 33% who traded political outcomes. The survey found that 10% of respondents had traded on a yes-or-no exchange over the previous year. Awareness remained limited: 42% had heard of prediction-market operators but had not used them, while 44% said they had never heard of prediction markets. BetMGM CEO Adam Greenblatt told analysts he expects the Supreme Court to rule against prediction markets and hopes the justices will clarify the issue during the 2026–2027 session. According to CDC Gaming, the court had not decided whether to hear the case, and its current term runs through June 2027. The CFTC has also proposed rulemaking concerning casino-style products on prediction markets, but that effort does not settle the live state cases. For operators, the immediate position is clearer: Google’s five named state exclusions remain in place while courts and regulators continue to contest who can oversee sports-event contracts. The Xbox Series X may stand out for its hardware, among the most powerful of the current generation of consoles, but it also offers useful features for different gaming habits. So, if you are interested in buying one, there are a few things you should know beyond the games it supports before investing in it instead of another console. So, even though Microsoft's Series X runs many games that you would also find available on the PS5, the experience on both consoles is still different. Sony's console has features Xbox doesn't offer, but it still has conveniences of its own. One is Quick Resume, which lets players quickly return to their games. To understand which details deserve attention before buying, we gathered some points that players consider important about the Xbox Series X. Some are benefits that may go unnoticed by people who do not know much about it, while others are limitations that could become a problem in the long run but, depending on your expectations, may not interfere much with the experience. Quick Resume is probably one of the most interesting perks of an Xbox Series X. It lets you switch between games compatible with this technology and return to where you left off in another one, without going through the opening sequence or initial menus again. So, you can start one game, open another, and then return to the first at the point where you were, without needing to save or do anything similar. This happens because the console stores the session state on the internal SSD, including what was happening at the time. So, if you need to stop playing for some reason or someone wants to try another game, you do not have to worry about losing your data or going back to an earlier point. Because the data stays on the SSD, it remains available even after you turn off the console or unplug it. However, even though the feature works well for most players, it can still fail. Quick Resume can still have issues, especially with games that require a server connection. So, even though reliability has improved through some updates, it is still worth keeping save files to avoid losing progress. Another strength of the Xbox Series X is its strong backward compatibility with games from previous console generations. So, you can run most Xbox One titles and a selection of Xbox 360 and original Xbox games on it. If you owned one of the previous-generation consoles and still have the games, you can still make use of those purchases. This includes classics like "Lost Odyssey" and "Blue Dragon," which may have gone overlooked. Some of these games also take advantage of the more powerful Xbox Series X hardware and receive some improvements. One is FPS Boost, which increases frame rates in selected games, while Auto HDR improves brightness in compatible titles. It also offers faster loading times and higher resolutions in certain games. "Fallout: New Vegas," for example, is among the titles with FPS Boost. Before buying older games, however, check the compatibility list and which discs the Series X accepts. The disc-drive version lets you use compatible physical media, while the original model relies on the account library, so even when a game is compatible, access is less broad. If you have more than one console, a few tricks let you use the same game library on two devices. One of them is setting another family member's Xbox as the home console for the account that buys the games. That way, they can access the titles with their own profile, while you play on your console with your own account, as long as you're connected to the internet. At the same time, both people can play the same game simultaneously without each person needing their own copy. This is one way to get more out of the Series X, especially if you do not want to spend money buying the same game twice. To enable the feature, sign in with the account that owns the games on the other console, then go to Settings > General > Personalization> My Home Xbox. You can also share games from a Game Pass subscription this way, but some benefits remain exclusive to the account owner. You can change the home console up to five times per year. You can also expand Xbox Series X storage with an external hard drive or SSD connected via USB, but it's not the same as an expansion card. It lets you store current-gen games and run many backward-compatible titles from it, freeing up space on the internal storage. However, most games optimized for Series X|S need to be installed on it or a supported expansion card to run, even if the USB device is also an SSD. In practice, you can use the USB device to store games you are not currently playing and transfer them back to the internal SSD when you want to play them again. This avoids re-downloading files, which helps anyone with slow internet or a data cap. Expansion cards, on the other hand, let you run games directly and offer performance equivalent to the internal storage. The best choice depends on how much you plan to spend and how many games you want to keep available without having to transfer files. If you plan to buy an Xbox Series X mainly to play console exclusives, you also need to consider that many of them are available on other platforms. For example, titles such as "Forza Horizon 5" and "Gears of War: Reloaded" are also available on PS5 and PC. This overlap is one of the disadvantages of buying an Xbox, especially if you already own another device that can run the games you want to play. However, Microsoft seems to be partially reversing this strategy and returning to some exclusives, at least on consoles. "Gears of War: E-Day" and "Clockwork Revolution" were among the games confirmed only for Xbox Series X|S and PC. So, in the future, the console may once again have some major games that justify buying it specifically for its exclusives. It also depends heavily on what you want. If you prioritize Nintendo franchises or certain PlayStation 5 exclusives, Xbox may not be the best option. It is also worth considering buying a gaming PC, since many Microsoft titles released for the Series X are also released on PC.

AIPlayStationPlayStation 6SonyVideo Game Industry  The next generation of home consoles is in constant fluctuation. Studio monopolies are caving in. Players are not on board with the all-digital future. One thing that is certain is that when Sony and Microsoft do pull the trigger, it will be monumentally expensive for players. With costs rising all over, consumer technology is among the fastest climbing expenses, with the AI boom hoovering up key computer components. According to one insider, the PlayStation 6âs memory alone will rake up more than $700 USD, pushing the full price tag over the $1,000 rim. According to Video Games Chronicle, AMD insider and forum poster âKeplerL2â believes that RAM and flash storage on Sonyâs next console will cost “over $680.” Itâs a startling number, a figure that once upon a time accounted for the entire package, but not a surprising one. Anyone who has had to pluck a quick SSD can attest how rapidly hardware costs have risen in the last three years. The prime mover in these mounting costs is the AI industry. These firms require monumental resources to dress a baby like a cop for TikTok videos. Before cement is even poured for data centers, companies are calling dibs on key suppliers like NVIDIA, meaning the costs youâre experiencing now is still a phantom to whatâs to come. Itâs forced many tech leaders, especially in the gaming space, to talk out of both sides of their mouth. Epicâs Tim Sweeney and Xboxâs Asha Sharma are laying the groundwork for gamingâs AI revolution five days of the week and admitting itâll lock out swaths of players on the sixth. Even before Sonyâs post-disc hostilities and fly by night tariffs, the very nature of the console market has shifted considerably. Once upon a time, these companies were willing to bite a loss on manufacturing, knowing they would make up for it with game sales and licensing fees. For over a generation, trends have shifted. Now the average player spends more time with fewer games. Subsidizing that loss with traditional game sales is no longer a guarantee. It has prompted the likes of Sony to focus its attention towards ventures like cross-media development and aspirations to take the live service space for themselves. Already the current generation of consoles, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and Nintendo Switch 2, are the first to uniformly become more expensive over time instead of less. How much further these costs will hike, and who will be able to keep up, is still in the making. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. By          Ryan Benk       ,          Ayesha Rascoe                        Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Virginia.                                                           Ryan Benk/NPR News                                       hide caption  The horror biz is booming, as recent Weekend Edition reporting has made clear. But not everyone wants to be up close and personal the with the IRL frights of a haunted house or spooky corn maze. Many would rather experience nightstalkers, goblins and witches that can't escape the theater or TV screen, or zombies and werewolves that won't lunge off the pages of a book. Chanthal Harris owns Long Dark House in Alexandria, Va. It's a bookstore devoted exclusively to horror and the supernatural. It's been doing business for just over a month and Harris says she already has steady traffic from both genre stalwarts and first-timers. "You know, I think people are looking for things that they wouldn't normally find in a lot of other places. I've had people comment about the curation and how they're finding something unexpected," Harris says. "And I'm also surprised at how many people are trying to dip their toe into horror." Harris is no newbie herself: books and horror have been constant companions. "My love of horror started from an early age. And I joke, but I do truly blame my parents because my dad was a[n] avid reader. He probably takes responsibility more for my fantasy/sci-fi love, but my mother always loved horror," Harris says. "To me it was completely normal. I didn't think of it as a spooky thing." So after a career in aviation, Harris decided to follow her passion and open Long Dark House. "It's exceeded my expectations and, you know, could be the season. But I just am so appreciative that people are as excited about these genres and this experience as I am. And so anytime someone walks through the door, I'm a little surprised and happy and grateful," she says. The numbers say Chanthal Harris shouldn't be very surprised. Market research by Nielsen says profits from the genre have jumped almost 26-percent year over year. And the numbers are good for films as well. Last May, Backrooms — about a horrifying liminal space that exists beyond our own reality — smashed box office records. With just a $10 million budget, petty cash for Hollywood, it grossed over $400 million worldwide. The feature film started as a short on YouTube. And It's just one title from the newly-merged studio Blumhouse Atomic Monster.                  Actor Chiwetel Umeadi Ejiofor portraying Clark in Backrooms.                                           A24/Blumhouse Atomic Monster                                       hide caption  Abhijay Prakash and Michael Clear head up the studio. Prakash is Blumhouse Atomic Monster's president and CEO. Clear is the president of Atomic Monster and leads the studio's emerging directors program. "We're drawn like moths to a flame to things that are scary," Clear says. "We reached out to Kane Parsons who had created the short and at the time he was 15 or 16; he was still in high school." Despite the headlines Blumhouse Atomic Monster garnered for hiring Parsons, Clear adds it's not really all that new for them. "We've always kind of scoured a variety of sources, particularly for filmmakers who have a sense of how to scare people. Going all the way back to one of the first movies we produced, Lights Out, David Sandberg, the director of that film, was actually himself a YouTube creator," Clear says. "They say it's hard to describe what scary is but I know it when I see it." A post-COVID reanimation? Abhijay Prakash says the COVID-19 pandemic had an outsized impact on the horror film industry. "Horror as a share of the box office…pre-COVID, was never more than 10% of the box office. Then after COVID though, it's occupying a much larger share. It's over 15%, almost 20% last year and this year. And inside of that we are over half of that box office," Prakash says. "So our market share is over 50% of the horror box office. And that's where we're focused. We live and breathe it." Our friends over at the Recreational Fear Lab theorize people are flocking to fear more these days because the real world has been just so darn scary. But Michael Clear thinks it could be a bit more complicated than that. "I agree it's part of it, but I also think that one of the things that shifted [is] the bar has been rising for what people need or what draws people to the theatres. It's been rising consistently over the last 10, 15 years," Clear says. "Maybe all the isolation has just driven people towards more social activities," he adds. "People are craving collective experiences. We're finding more now than before the pandemic that people are going to movies in larger groups. And it just so happens that our genre, because it's participatory — if we do our jobs right, we're getting reactions, audible reactions from the audience — and it can be more fun to experience that with your friends." "Scary stories in the dark," Abhijay Prakash underlines. "[It] has delivered for thousands of years." It has to be "real" While Blumhouse Atomic Monster makes its bid to reign supreme in theaters, many scream queens and kings are finding bite-sized horror scrolling social media. And often, those scary shorts are the products of AI. "Personally, I think that, you know, anything that makes filmmaking more democratic can can be great. You know, people who find tools that can enable them to create it will allow more people, more talented people, to enter the space," Michael Clear says. He cautions that audiences want things to feel authentic, as though the horror on the screen is genuine. "When it comes to our movies, I think one of the things that just happens to be a characteristic of our genre is that the things that are scariest are the things that feel the most real. So really, when you get down to the way that AI images or whatever may impact movies, you know, our focus is always on doing things as real as possible. Doing things as practically as possible," Clear says. The 'Disney of horror' Abhijay Prakash told The Ankler early this year that his goal for Blumhouse Atomic Monster is to be the Disney of fear. He breaks down what he means: "Every place that consumers engage with scary stories is a place that we as a business, as a company obsessed with horror and scary stories will be. And then it's only a question of the business model," Prakash says. Prakash says the studio is exploring creating an attraction from its Five Nights at Freddy's franchise and he also points to the popularity of the stage version of Paranormal Activity. "So that really is a guiding principle for our company. We want to be everywhere where horror is relevant and it's taking a bigger and bigger place in the culture," Prakash says. Michael Clear says the idea isn't just to cater to existing fans of the genre, but to grow the fanbase for all things spooky itself. "We like to think that we can provide a kind of gateway horror," he says. Next week we get a lesson in horror storytelling from one of the most prolific writers in the genre — Stephen Graham Jones. Tech > Mobile Eligible recipients in the class action settlement can now sign up for payouts over Apple's AI lawsuit. Senior Writer Senior Writer October 18, 2026, 2:00 pm ET Apple is settling a lawsuit related to the delayed rollout of Apple Intelligence features. The iPhone 16 went on sale in September 2024 with Apple Intelligence at the center of its marketing. However, the first AI features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, several weeks later, and the most heavily promoted one, a Siri that could pull personal context from your apps, was delayed in March 2025. That’s the basis of a $250 million class action settlement that’s now accepting claims. Eligible buyers have until Dec. 21 to file, and each qualifying iPhone gets its own claim. Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The form to opt-in is available only for a limited time, though, so get your name into the pool before it closes. Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected. “Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET. The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months. “False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history. Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website. The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.  If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment: The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features. It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement. When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later. According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.” Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September. According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court. After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment. On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027. Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. The SEC’s new framework for trading tokenized stocks is encountering resistance from some of the companies whose shares could trade, with Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ) and UnitedHealth (UNH) among the latest issuers to object. Eight newly disclosed objections appeared in an October 15 public notice from OKXICE, the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) preparing to offer tokenized stock trading. Alongside Broadcom, Verizon and UnitedHealth, the notice names AppLovin (APP), Applied Digital (APLD), Rocket Lab (RKLB), CoreWeave (CRWV) and Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI). It lists nine objecting issuers in total, including AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems (CBRS), which formally opted out of being listed earlier. The update did not disclose why the companies objected or when they submitted their notices. Nasdaq (NDAQ) has separately said it would opt out of having its own shares tokenized under the framework, according to an FAQ on its website. A Nasdaq spokesperson told the Wall Street Journal that the company does not want its shares trading on a venue that does not display best prices in real time or report to the consolidated tape, which aggregates stock-market trading data. Nasdaq is not among the nine issuers named in OKXICE’s notice. OKXICE announced on October 5 that it had notified the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission of plans to launch the venue, initially targeting shares of 63 U.S.-listed companies. Former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, the venture’s co-chair, announced the move on X. The venue would operate under the SEC’s five-year “Innovation Exemption,” issued September 17, which allows qualifying platforms to trade tokenized U.S. stocks using automated market makers and liquidity pools. Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based representations of shares. OKXICE plans to operate around the clock using Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, with trades settled in stablecoins. Under the model described in its notice, underlying shares would be held one-for-one against outstanding tokens through a registered broker-dealer. Token holders must receive equivalent rights, including dividends and voting rights. The issuer pushback echoes findings from TD Securities analysts led by Reid Noch, vice president of U.S. equity market structure. Conversations with dozens of issuers showed “little interest in tokenizing their shares outside a small group of crypto-adjacent companies,” the analysts wrote in a report shared with CoinDesk. Several issuers also approached the firm with significant concerns after discovering the framework, having been unaware of it when it was announced, the report said. TD Securities named the framework’s reliance on temporary exemptive relief, rather than permanent rules, as its largest hurdle. A future commission could reverse the approach, complicating the case for investing in infrastructure and discouraging institutions from integrating with venues even after they launch, the analysts said. That uncertainty is especially challenging when overseas platforms can continue offering synthetic stock products without assuming the operational requirements of the U.S. relief, they added. A sudden wave of selling wiped out nearly $52 million in crypto traders’ leveraged bets on chip stocks in 10 minutes on Saturday, while the shares themselves sat idle with Wall Street closed for the weekend. Those bets were placed through perpetual futures, contracts that track a stock’s price and trade around the clock on crypto exchanges, so traders can buy and sell chip stocks on a Saturday night.  A trader who borrows to make a bigger bet gets closed out automatically when losses eat through their deposit, and the forced selling can push prices lower for the next trader in line. About $51.6 million in positions tied to chip stocks and semiconductor funds were force-closed between 21:22 and 21:32 UTC, according to CoinGlass data, and about $38 million of that came from traders betting on higher prices. SOXL, a fund that triples the daily moves in chip shares, took the biggest hit at about $12.7 million. SanDisk and SK Hynix contracts followed at about $10.8 million each. The selling started on Binance, according to a review of the trades by David Jeong, chief executive of trading firm Tread.fi, who placed the first large SanDisk and Micron sell orders on Binance at 21:21:59 UTC. Less than a second later, orders hit Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange where Trade XYZ lists stock-tracking contracts, and roughly 10 addresses opened bets against six chip-linked contracts within 1.8 seconds. Binance handled about $21.9 million of SanDisk trading in that first minute, against $3.1 million on Trade XYZ. Memory-chip shares were already coming off a rough week as investors weighed new competition from Chinese chipmaker CXMT. With the stock market shut, there was no real share price for these contracts to follow, so traders were reacting only to each other. Trade XYZ’s rules let trading on the platform set its own reference prices until outside stock quotes come back. Those quotes return when U.S. markets open Monday, which will show how far Saturday’s prices strayed from where the shares actually trade. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Melanie Dulbecco, the CEO of syrup brand Torani. She's based in San Leandro, California, where the company is headquartered. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I may sound different than most CEOs. I grew up in a blue-collar neighborhood, and my parents divorced when I was really young. When I was little, I saw my mom struggle so much, and I noticed that some kids around me didn't have the same opportunities. I felt this sense of inequity, and that became a motivating and driving force for me. I tried working in politics, then nonprofits, and eventually went into business. I wanted to build an opportunity company. When I met the family from Torani, they liked that idea. I was the ninth hire at Torani in 1991 and became the first CEO in 1995. We now have over 500 employees. When I started, we made $700,000 a year in annual revenue. We've grown 20% a year on average, and this year, we plan to hit over $800 million in revenue. But to us, growth is not a financial endeavor. The trailing indicator of success may be the financials, but we think our work together creates the momentum and value in the marketplace that drives our growth. It's very easy for us to say layoffs are not our approach. I think layoffs are a choice. I get it if a company is going through bankruptcy and has to make extremely challenging choices. Otherwise, I think it's a financial exercise that doesn't consider how you're going to be resilient or regain momentum — because you do that with a team. Torani is currently hiring fewer people than it would be if the company didn't use automation. We use automation to deprioritize manual, rote jobs with limited career mobility. We also use AI for consumer and market research, sales forecasting, and demand planning. Create a BI Job Scout and get opportunities matched to your goals. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    However, our team doesn't get worried about things like AI because they trust that we will both automate and elevate the work, that we will never do anything that squashes opportunities for people, and that we are looking out for everybody's success. We're often in hyper-growth mode, which means we need people to know how to work together. The ability to work together, to collaborate, to address challenges, to be resilient in tough times, is critical. This strategy has also helped with retention. We had been planning a move to our new location in San Leandro in March 2020. That happened to coincide with the stay-at-home order. It was one of those moments where, as a leader, you feel like you have to breathe into a paper bag. We had borrowed a lot of money from the bank to build our new flavor factory. The loans were going to start coming due in April, so the executive team came together to look at what we needed to do to be OK. Before we did that, though, we asked: What will make us proud when we get to the other side of this? We had a long discussion about it and decided that making it as one team — without any layoffs or furloughs — would make us proud. So we we scaled back marketing and advertising expenses and paused all company travel. All departments had to review their budgets. They got scrappy to identify and eliminate non-essential costs. During the early months of the pandemic, Torani prepared for a 50% decline in sales. Thankfully, there was only a 20% decline in April of 2020, and revenue was back up in May. We quickly pivoted to online retail and grocery to fill the gaps left by cafés and drink shops closing their doors. Torani ended 2020 with a 15% year-over-year revenue increase. We moved to our new location in six months instead of six weeks, but we got there. We couldn't have done that if we laid off our team. We needed to come together at that moment. US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table". Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened. Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake". Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed. In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now". Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%. In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders". Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia. Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks. Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues. Login  Peter  18 October 2026   Weekly poll OnePlus  The OnePlus 15 was the last global flagship from the company. Since it launched, OnePlus left the global market to focus only on India and China. Well, mostly on China – this week, the company announced the OnePlus 16 for the Chinese market. As for India, there is conflicting information on whether or not the 16 will be available. One tipster claims that the company will launch the cheaper OnePlus 16R and that it “might” launch the full-fat 16 flagship too. So, this might be an exercise in futility, but what do you think about the OnePlus 16? Would you buy one if you had the chance? Before you answer, let’s look at the upgrades.     OnePlus 16 color options  The new model upgrades to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, up from the Elite Gen 5. It starts with 12GB/256GB memory and has upgrades all the way to 16GB/1TB. This generation also brings a larger 9,000mAh Si/C battery (up from 7,300mAh on the previous model) with 100W wired and 50W wireless charging. The company also equipped the OnePlus 16 with its first-ever 200MP sensor (1/1.4”). It also has a larger 1/1.95” sensor in the telephoto camera (vs. 1/2.76”), but with a slightly shorter 3x lens (73mm vs. 80mm). There’s a 50MP ultra-wide camera on the back and a 50MP ultra-wide selfie camera (18mm lens) on the front. The display is a 6.78” 185Hz LTPO panel from BOE. Well, it runs at 165Hz most of the time with only a select few games supporting the full 185Hz.     OnePlus 16 Sounds like an awesome phone and if you are in China, you can get one for CNY 6,000 – that is how much a 12GB/256GB unit costs. Okay, this might sound like sour grapes, but we don’t love the 50% price hike – the 12GB/256GB OnePlus 15 launched at CNY 4,000 last year. Even the 16GB/1TB model was only CNY 5,400. The global 12GB/256GB model launched at $900 / £850 / €950 / ₹73,000, so a 50% increase over those prices would have made it a tough sell. And keep in mind that the Chinese prices are usually better than the global ones. Following its launch in China, the Oppo Find X10 series will launch in India next week. For the sake of comparison, we’ll note that the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is 13% more expensive at CNY 6,800 for a 12GB/256GB unit. The Oppo Find X10 and Find X10 Pro Max will be available globally, by the way, not just in China and India, unlike the OnePlus 16. So, what do you think – are you sorry that the OnePlus 16 isn’t available globally? And if you are in India, would you consider the OnePlus 16 if it indeed launches in the country? This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Andrew Koller, 31, a freelance camera operator who purchased a home in Yamagata, Japan, in March. Koller, who's based in Edmonton, Canada, renovated the home and plans to use it as a vacation home. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Like a lot of millennials, I was exposed to Japanese culture in some sense early on with "Naruto," "Pokemon," and "Dragon Ball Z." After that, I don't think my interest really left. Come 2020, I had a bunch of time on my hands like everybody else. It seemed like a good time to finally learn Japanese. I've been learning Japanese with a private tutor since then. Then, in 2023, I made my first trip to Japan. Like everybody else who comes back from their first trip to Japan, I just fell in love. I couldn't stop talking about it, but I wanted a deeper connection to the community. I wanted more than just the superficial, surface-level experience of Japanese life. So I thought maybe a good way to get that experience would be to buy a house that's not in a major tourist city, somewhat live there, and spend a good chunk of time over there getting involved with the community by renovating a forgotten property. The algorithm was watching for sure. After my first Japan trip, my YouTube and Instagram algorithms were suggesting to me all these similar people doing similar things. From that, I was like, this seems like something I can do. In my free time, I like to DIY. I have a little workshop — I wouldn't say I'm good at it, but I feel like I know enough to do the basics. I'm at the point in my life now where I've had all these ideas and I've said, "Oh, it'd be cool to do this," but I never do it. I never follow through. I just wanted to prove to myself that I actually followed through on one of these somewhat whimsical ideas. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    I've always been interested in real estate since a young age.  Purchasing your first house is doable, but if you want to purchase a second house after that, like a rental, it's extremely challenging to do that in Canada. Canada's housing market has exploded, especially in Alberta. I'm in a very fortunate position where my partner and I own a house and we own a rental property as well close to the university area. I bought the rental house when I was 20 with my parents — they had to sign on because no bank was going to loan a 20-year-old kid a mortgage. I rented out the rooms and then I lived for free for my time in college. Both houses have a similar value. My primary residence is worth just under $600,000 CAD (about $422,880). When we bought the rental 10 years ago, it was around $500,000 CAD, but it's gone up since. For my home in Japan, I spent $15,000 CAD (about $10,600) on the purchase price plus closing costs, which was another $3,000 CAD. I can definitely see myself spending extended time in Japan. I want to go out there at least a few times a year. It's close to a pretty big ski resort, and I snowboard. Doing the math for that, if I was to go stay in Banff or Jasper — one of the more popular mountain towns in Alberta — for a week and ski, it's actually cheaper to fly to Japan, because the skiing is also very affordable, so that was a big factor for me. I went to Japan in October 2025 to look at properties. I made an offer in November, it got accepted, and then I got possession of the property in March 2026. Then I went up for the entire month of April to start renovations on it. I wanted to respect what was already there when I went in. Even though the house itself wasn't ancient or historical — it was built in the '60s or '70s — it was very traditionally built with the Tatami rooms. I wanted to keep a lot of that, coming in as a Westerner. I wanted to try and adapt to their way of life rather than trying to impose my own. I just wanted to complement what was already there. Now, the house is 98% done. The actual renovation costs right now are just over the purchase cost. So I'm at around $18,000 CAD and change, doing most of it myself. Right now, the goal would be to do a short-term rental in the future, but I don't plan on it making a lot of money. I think that's the one thing people will get confused about. They think, "If I do this and renovate it, I can make a ton of money off a short-term rental in Japan." That's not the case, because there's so much competition with the hotels there that are already amazing and very affordable. I just want to cover the maintenance costs more than anything. Doing a little bit of short-term rental, I think, will help with that. It's not an asset. I think maybe people go to Japan with the Western mindset, like, "Oh, it's a buy-and-hold asset." Outside of Tokyo and the big cities, real estate doesn't do that. Real estate always goes down in value over time. If you're buying a house in Japan, go in with the expectation that it's not as much of a financial asset as it is a recreation: you'll get more of a cultural experience. At last month's White House AI Summit, some of the richest individuals on Earth were clustered around US President Donald Trump. Each of them had built their fortune in the tech industry. Some of the biggest names at the table were major players well before the AI boom began, such as the leaders of Amazon, Meta and SpaceX. Others have risen in prominence in the past few years, such as those representing AI labs including Anthropic and OpenAI. And then there were the chip makers, selling computing power to a frenzy of data centre operators around the world. They are making the picks and shovels of the AI boom. One of them is Jensen Huang. He is the CEO of Nvidia, which sells a large share of the world's top-tier AI chips. He has been described as the most powerful man in AI. Lisa Su was the only woman among the AI executives. She is the CEO of another chip maker, AMD. Micron Technology CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has overseen a spectacular rise as demand for computing power took off. Taken together, the group's estimated net worth is north of $2.5 trillion. (Keep in mind, we're using Australian dollars throughout this story.) Anthropic and OpenAI are private companies, so you won't find them on the stock exchange. However, most of the listed companies in the AI space have seen their stock prices soaring in recent months. Steve Johnson, chief investment officer of investment fund Forager, said AI companies were some of the fastest-growing businesses the world's ever seen. "We've never seen anything like it," he said. In the US, these AI-related companies have become so huge that they are comparable to the banks and mining companies in Australia's market, Mr Johnson said. But their success has not been replicated across all parts of the US economy. Some experts point to how the AI boom is masking weaknesses elsewhere, and how its outsized influence on the market may bring risks all of its own. Let's take a look at why. Here is a map of the S&P 500 — the top 500 listed companies in the US. The size of each box corresponds to an individual company's market capitalisation. That's the combined value of all its shares (or, to oversimplify a bit, how much it is worth overall). Tech stocks dominate the market, accounting for about 44 per cent of the total value. Six of the eight biggest US companies are in the tech industry — and that's using a narrow enough definition that it excludes Amazon and Tesla. AI chip maker Nvidia is the most valuable company in the world, worth about $7.5 trillion. But size is not the only factor that matters. Over the past six months, four companies grew more than Nvidia (in absolute terms). In order, they were: Apple, Microsoft, Micron and AMD. To see just how much their stock prices have increased … let's switch to 3D. The height of each box now shows how much each company's stock price has increased or decreased in the past six months. That means their 3D size (or volume) represents their change in overall value. It may not look like it, but Apple has grown the most. It grew by 30 per cent, rising by more than $1.4 trillion in just six months. Micron and AMD have more than doubled their valuation in the past six months, leaving their boxes tall yet narrow. About 230 of the 500 stocks on the S&P 500 have seen their stock prices go down since April. They lost a combined $2.9 trillion in value. However, their losses were offset by the combined gains of just Meta, Microsoft and Apple. Add in the other three biggest winners — Micron, Nvidia and AMD — and you have already accounted for 57 per cent of the S&P 500's total gains since April. Together, these six companies have grown by more than $5 trillion in that time. Take these away, and the overall market would look very different. Without the growth of these six companies, the S&P 500 would have grown just 4.35 per cent in the past six months — that is less than half the actual figure of 10 per cent. The dominance of a single sector is not new, but the scale of market concentration is becoming unusual, RMIT economics expert Angel Zhong says. "At the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000, the top 10 stocks made up about 27 per cent of the S&P 500. Recently, it is about 39 per cent," she said. Unlike during the dot-com bubble — when crazy valuations were based largely on hype — some AI companies are already highly profitable. Chip makers Nvidia, Micron and AMD all fall into that category. But this is not true across the board. "Revenue at the leading AI labs is still a fraction of what is being spent on their behalf," Professor Zhong said. And these AI labs — such as OpenAI and Anthropic — are among the biggest customers of the chip makers and the data centre operators. The other major buyers are the tech giants going all-in on AI, including Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet (that's Google). Their staggering levels of investment are outpacing their world-beating profits. "This boom started out being paid for mostly from profits," Professor Zhong said. "Now it increasingly relies on outside money, including a lot of debt." Another concern is where this outside money is coming from. Nvidia has been called the "bank of AI", since it is investing hundreds of billions of dollars in its biggest customers. This means massive sums of money are essentially going around in circles. Here's one such example: This is just one example of many, Professor Zhong said. "[These] companies are each other's investors, suppliers and customers at the same time. "It's harder to tell how much AI demand is genuine and how much is funded by the sellers themselves." This ties the companies' fortunes together. "If one key player, especially OpenAI, ran into trouble, the effects would ripple through the whole network," Professor Zhong said. And, as we have seen, this network of AI-related companies now represents a major part of the entire S&P 500. And that could expand even further if OpenAI and Anthropic proceed with their plans to go public and list on the stock market. While Forager's Steve Johnson is quick to point out the risks of this concentrated AI-heavy market, he agrees the technology has the potential to change the world. "There's no doubt about AI's impact on the broader economy. It is going to be a part of our everyday lives." But that does not necessarily translate into returns for those who invest in it. "The question is whether these are going to be great businesses or not … I think the technology can be transformational, and people [can] still not do well from the investments." It all comes down to whether these companies — the AI labs, the chip makers, the data centre operators and the tech giants — can collectively turn a promising new technology into a money maker that matches the massive sums being invested. "I think from an investor perspective, the hype around this is almost certain to end in disappointment," Mr Johnson said. "It's going to be very fascinating to see how it unfolds." With just over a week to go until Israel’s election day, President Donald Trump finally gave the full-throated endorsement that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had long sought.                   The president called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a post on social media, which he said serves as his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.”                   Trump also hinted at a possible resumption of hostilities in the unpopular war with Iran — a war the US launched alongside Israel eight months ago — saying that if the Iranians do not “change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job.”                   Netanyahu was quick to respond, thanking Trump for the “tremendous support and the joint work.”                   Trump told Axios journalist and CNN Global Affairs analyst Barak Ravid in a brief phone interview that he had always intended to endorse Netanyahu. “I was always going to do that. I just didn’t want to do it too soon,” he said.                   Trump added that they have a “good relationship” and would “continue to do well” together if Netanyahu is reelected, according to Ravid.                   “It is important that Israel has a person they can count on,” Trump said.                   It was an endorsement that seemed uncertain until it finally arrived and cannot mask what has become at times a rocky relationship between the two.                   For years, Israelis driving the country’s highways in the final weeks of an election have seen the same image: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu standing beside President Donald Trump, under the slogan, “A different league.”                   Less than two weeks before the October 27 vote, the billboards of Netanyahu are back. But this time Trump is not on them.                   The president still appears in some videos for Netanyahu’s Likud party, but his absence may signal something beyond advertising.                   Until Sunday, Trump had held off endorsing Netanyahu.                   “I’m not involved in [Israeli] politics anymore,” he told Time earlier this month. On Thursday, Trump told Newsmax that Netanyahu would like him to be involved in the election. “I’ve had a very good relationship with him,” he said, but avoided endorsing him again. When asked directly whether he trusts Netanyahu, he said bluntly, “I don’t trust anybody in the world of politics.”                   Trump has starred in Netanyahu’s campaigns since 2013, when still a businessman and TV personality, he released a video urging Israelis to “vote for Benjamin.”                   When Trump entered the White House in 2017, he showered Netanyahu with political gifts.                   About two weeks before Israel’s April 2019 election, Netanyahu was in Washington to watch Trump sign a historic proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights. In January 2020, five weeks before Israelis went again to the polls, Trump unveiled the Israeli-Palestinian “Deal of the Century” plan. Netanyahu stood smiling by his side.                   Ahead of this election, there has been no red carpet. The last time Netanyahu and Trump met at the White House in August, there were no cameras. The two did not meet at all when Netanyahu traveled to New York for the UN General Assembly in September.                   Over the course of the last year, Netanyahu has taken steps that have drawn fury from Trump, including undermining Trump-led peace efforts by striking inside Lebanon and Gaza.                   Trump has cursed the prime minister out in phone calls and warned him he’s losing support among Americans, according to people familiar with the conversations. He’s asked why Israel was blowing up apartment buildings in Lebanon and warned about the risk of a global economic downturn as a result of the Iran war.                   Inside the White House, many of the moves were interpreted as election-year posturing by Netanyahu, whose internal politics are well known by Trump and his advisers. Over the summer, many Trump advisers came to the conclusion that Netanyahu was trying to prolong the Iran war to bolster his own political standing.                   Trump has given Netanyahu a degree of leeway because of those political concerns, people familiar with the matter said. But he’s still grown frustrated at some of Israel’s actions, many of which he believes run counter to American interests.                   Another person close to Trump suggested his lack of endorsement had been tied to Netanyahu’s weakness in the polls. Trump has long been careful to avoid endorsing candidates who seem likely to lose.                   In conversations over the past several months, Trump has quizzed Netanyahu about the election and his prospects, according to people familiar with the matter. While Netanyahu has sought to project confidence, Trump is well aware of the prime minister’s difficult political position.                   As Netanyahu’s standing fell in the Trump administration, so did Trump’s standing in Israel.                   According to Israeli sources close to Netanyahu, Trump was originally meant to be a centerpiece of Netanyahu’s campaign. Last December, at Mar-a-Lago, the prime minister announced that Trump would become the first non-Israeli to receive the prestigious Israel Prize. Netanyahu aides hoped Trump would accept the prize in person at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony in April, giving jumpstarting the campaign.                   Then came the war with Iran.                   The joint US-Israeli attack began on February 28 with the two leaders projecting strategic harmony. Netanyahu thanked “my friend, President Donald Trump,” calling him “a leader who stands by his word.” Trump described the two of them as “war heroes” and publicly demanded that Israel’s president grant Netanyahu a pardon in his ongoing corruption trials.       ‘This was communicated at every level’: Netanyahu military aide reveals internal warnings before October 7               But Trump never showed interest in attending the Israel Prize ceremony. By then, the fighting in Iran had ended and ceasefire talks were underway.                   The Iran ceasefire and subsequent memorandum of understanding were deeply unpopular in Israel, particularly on the right. Yinon Magal, a pro-Netanyahu TV anchor, called Trump a “loser” after the deal was signed.                   A July survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute found that only 7% of Israelis had “a great deal of trust” that Trump “will do the right thing” on US-Israel relations, and 45% had none.                   “Trump’s stock in Israel, especially among right wing-voters, has weakened,” a Likud source said. “An endorsement would not necessarily have helped Netanyahu so much, so he did not invest much in it.” Another Likud source said, “It’s not as if Trump will endorse any other opponent, so it’s nice to have, but not a must.”                   Netanyahu’s opponents are watching, but with less alarm than before. “A year ago, our camp was calling anyone close to Trump to prevent an endorsement,” one senior opposition figure said ahead of Sunday’s news. “Now it doesn’t really matter, the charm is not there.”                   When Trump was asked specifically about who is currently polling as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, he said, “Well, I don’t know, I don’t hear bad things about him.” He then said, “They’ve written Bibi off many, many times, just like they’ve written me off many, many times. I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.”                   Trump has his own reasons for distance. American public opinion of Israel has fallen sharply, declining even more against the backdrop of the Iran war. Israel’s average net favorability fell from +51 points in July 2018 to -16 in July 2026, according to multiple polls, a 67-point drop over eight years.                   As America quickly soured on the Iran war, a source familiar with the relationship said, Trump has been “trying to shed the image that Netanyahu pulled him into it.”                   Still, the apparent distance may be misleading. Israeli sources say the two leaders have recently discussed renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli security sources told CNN preparations are underway - pending Trump’s decision - with timing unclear because of the US midterm elections.                   Netanyahu rejected suggestions he was seeking escalation before the vote.                   “It is not convenient for us, it’s no good,” he told Army Radio this week. He complained that if Iran fired missiles at Israel, his opponents “will blame me.”      © 2026 Cable News Network. All Rights Reserved.  CNN Sans ™ & © 2016 Cable News Network.
