Sudanese are facing growing costs of medicine caused by the country’s civil war. Save Share Hasanat al-Rashid, 48, has lived with diabetes for 15 years, and the three-and-a-half-year civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group has worsened her situation. Finding the treatment she needs has become a daily struggle. When the war broke out in April 2023, she was forced to flee south from her home in Haj Yousif in Khartoum North to Umm Daw Ban in Khartoum State. During her displacement, she went for days without medication and was forced to eat foods unsuitable for her condition, such as asida, a traditional Sudanese porridge. She underwent operations on her foot twice when she developed complications of diabetes, including a severe infection. She moved between hospitals in Gezira State south of Khartoum, seeking treatment in Rufaa, Wad Madani and Al-Hasahisa. When fighting spread to these areas in December 2023, she fled again, arriving in Port Sudan, a city on the Red Sea that was less affected by the war. Her condition has worsened to the point that she now has to use insulin every day and with this comes added costs, something that forces diabetes sufferers in Sudan to choose between medicine and other essentials, such as food. “The doses vary depending on whether my blood sugar is high or low,” she told Al Jazeera. The war has pushed income levels in Sudan back to those last seen in the 1990s, according to the United Nations Development Programme. This means Hasanat and other diabetes sufferers are struggling to afford the medicine they need to treat the condition. Hasanat’s doctor recommended she use an insulin pen, a device used to inject insulin under the skin. She would need one or two of the devices a month, but the cost at 70,000 Sudanese pounds ($8) is more than she can afford up front, so she opts for a vial of insulin. This is cheaper at 17,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.80), but there is the additional cost of buying ice every day to keep the insulin cool. She spends 180,000 pounds ($20) a month on ice to preserve the medicine. But she is able to spread these costs out through the month, making the vials her only viable option even if the overall costs are higher than an insulin pen. “It may last a month or less, but the challenge is that I don’t have a refrigerator, so I struggle to store the insulin properly,” she said. She also needs painkillers and vitamins on a regular basis to manage complications caused by the diabetes. Fatima Adam, 75, is among the patients at Port Sudan Hospital struggling to afford the medicines she needs to manage her hypertension and a thyroid condition. She was admitted to the hospital with complications caused by high blood pressure, which has started to impact her heart. Too unwell to speak to Al Jazeera herself, her daughter, Aisha, described how the rising cost of treatment has affected her whole family. Before the war, Fatima received medicine through the National Health Insurance Fund. She paid a quarter of the cost while the fund covered the rest. But when the war started and the economy collapsed, the medicines she needed were no longer covered by the scheme. “My mother takes six different medicines because hypertension has affected her heart in addition to her thyroid medication. The war has made things harder because the prices of these medicines have gone up,” Aisha told Al Jazeera. The responsibility for paying for Fatima’s treatment and supporting her and her daughter falls on her son, who works as a casual worker. With no fixed income, he goes to the market every day in search of work but sometimes returns home empty without any luck. “Sometimes, when my brother finds work, we buy enough medicine to last a month. Other times, we have to buy smaller quantities and take the medicines intermittently,” Aisha said. She bought a month’s supply of her mother’s medication a few days ago for 160,000 Sudanese pounds ($17.80), a substantial expense for a family whose income depends on day labour but essential to treating Fatima’s condition. The war has caused an estimated $500m in losses to medicine stocks, infrastructure and transport fleets, dealing a major blow to Sudan’s pharmaceutical supply system, the National Medical Supplies Fund told Al Jazeera. The National Medicines and Poisons Board estimated that only eight of the 30 pharmaceutical factories in Khartoum that shut down during the conflict have resumed operations despite the security situation in the capital recently improving. This has increased Sudan’s reliance on imported medicines, but the subsequent depreciation of the Sudanese pound has driven up the costs of pharmaceutical procurement and production. Hossam al-Naeem, who works as a pharmacist in Port Sudan, said customers with diabetes and hypertension require regular painkillers and vitamins to help their overall condition. “I feel deeply saddened when I see the expressions on some patients’ faces as they ask about the prices of medicines and discover how much they have increased because of the depreciation of the Sudanese pound,” Hossam told Al Jazeera. The currency’s collapse has created added challenges for pharmacists. Before the war, a dollar traded for roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Now black-market currency traders are quoting rates of 9,300 pounds to the dollar, meaning higher costs for most goods in Sudan. Sometimes Hossam incurs losses himself when he finds that the prices of drugs have risen sharply, and keeping essential medicines stocked is becoming difficult. “I used to sell a strip of cold and flu tablets for 6,000 Sudanese pounds [70 cents]. But when I went to buy new stock, I found that the supplier’s price was also 6,000 pounds per strip. That means I made no profit, not even enough to cover the pharmacy’s operating costs,” he said. Huda Mahmoud, 58, lives in el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state in south-central Sudan, where drone attacks and other violence remain a problem while the military is making advances towards the city. Huda has lived with heart problems for more than 12 years and described the impacts of the war as being physical, financial and emotional. “I take five different medicines. There was a time when they weren’t available, and I suffered a lot. Sometimes, I had to ask people in Wad Madani, Sennar or Port Sudan to send them to me,” she told Al Jazeera. “The medicines were extremely expensive, costing me 300,000 Sudanese pounds [$33.30] a month.” Taking medication has become a carefully managed routine with each pill tied to a specific time of day. “I’ve become tied to my pills: this one before eating, that one afterwards. If I forget one, my heart starts beating very fast,” she added. In March, Huda was forced to travel from el-Obeid to Omdurman. Following her strict treatment regimen has become increasingly difficult during repeated periods of upheaval. She has now returned home to el-Obeid, where her regular medicine is priced at 151,000 Sudanese pounds ($16.80) a month, something she can barely afford. Her greatest fear is running out of medicine or being unable to afford her next supply, which would put her at risk of a blood clot. “I’m afraid of becoming incapacitated. I used to be responsible for the whole household, but now I need help. I feel like I’ve become a burden on my family,” she said.          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX index, ripped higher on Friday as stocks tanked on AI and geopolitical worries. Bitcoin BTC$82,001.05 traded in a choppy manner as well.  Traders are betting the fear gauge keeps climbing. However, if VIX history and bitcoin’s steady weekend price action are any guide, the panic could subside just as quickly on Monday. First, a quick primer. Cboe’s VIX measures how much traders expect the S&P 500, the blue-chip stock index, to swing over the next four weeks. It's derived from options prices. When people get nervous, they buy options, which are contracts used to hedge against price swings. That pushes the VIX up. Bitcoin BTC$82,001.05, meanwhile, is the only macro asset thats trades over the weekend. As such, swings in bitcoin over the weekend are often seen as lead indicators of how traditional markets may open on Monday.  On Friday, the VIX jumped 21.5% to 19.99 as the S&P 500 fell by 1.09%.  That's VIX’s biggest one-day rise since June 5, when the S&P 500 suffered its worst day in months, according to data source TradingView. Traders are betting the VIX stays high through November. CNBC reports that traders bought 9,200 of the Nov. 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million. Traders also bought 12,500 of the Nov. 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million. The bet is that the VIX closes above 23 by the third week of November. That sentiment is consistent with the present macro developments. AI stocks have been hit hard in the week gone by. The cost of default insurance on AI-related firms has hit record highs. Geopolitics is pushing oil higher too. On Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The Russia-Ukraine front looks like it's heating up as well. Big Friday jumps in the VIX usually don't last, according to historical data. CoinDesk's analysis of the data finds the VIX has jumped 20% or more on a Friday 32 times since January 1990, not counting the latest one. The next Monday, it fell 25 times and rose just seven.  In other words, investors slept over the Friday panic over the weekend and things normalized on Monday. The typical  Monday move was a drop of 4.5%. A month later, the VIX was lower in 25 of the 32 cases, and the median drop was 16%. Seasonality also favors the VIX bears, and by extension stock market stability.  The VIX has declined in November in 25 of the last 36 years, with a median drop of 7.2%. From October end to the end of the year, VIX has fallen in 22 of 36 years, with a median decline of 9.4%. Bitcoin isn’t flinching. It continues to trade above $80,000, comfortably within its recent choppy range, suggesting Friday’s risk aversion and VIX rise may not carry into Monday. The bitcoin market has been more active over the weekend this year, especially on Sunday, as geopolitical flareups that began in early March keep investors on edge. That activity highlights bitcoin’s role as a always-on macro asset: When traditional markets are shut, traders use bitcoin to express their early read on global risk appetite. Volmex's BVIV, the bitcoin volatility index, or the bitcoin VIX, slipped 1% on Friday to just under 40% and has barely moved since. BVIV shows the 30-day implied or expected volatility in bitcoin. Bettors on the decentralized platform Polymarket aren't panicking either. They see just an 9% chance the AI bubble bursts this year as of this writing.  None of the above guarantees a stable Monday. Moreover, in seven of the 32 cases, the VIX kept climbing sharply on Monday, including in August 2015, February 2018 and August 2024. Going purely by the VIX levels, there's room for the index to run.  Even after Friday’s spike, the VIX is still under 20, a mark it has topped on more than a third of days since 1990. It has closed above 30 on just 8% of days. So, if fear grips the market further on Monday morning, the VIX can climb. At 9 p.m. on a recent Friday night, Max Harding had just returned from a barefoot run in the woods. The eccentric 20-year-old Californian was back in a large barn in rural Pennsylvania — still barefoot — alternatively working on his startup and asking me about the point of life. Though not an especially adept programmer, Harding possesses a more adroit, perhaps unteachable skill that has never been more valuable in the current landscape of founder culture. "Max captures the attention of the camera, keeps us center stage," said his cofounder, Skyler Ji, who added that Harding's role includes "spreading our philosophy" while he runs the operation behind the scenes. "Max brings some of the grander things," Ji told me. The pair's startup, Hivemind Research, aims to build "digital brains" in the form of social media. Harding and Ji were among 66 mostly young, mostly imaginative startup founders taking part in a two-week "incubator" workshop called Launchpad. The novel event was hosted by Stan, the company behind a moderately successful platform for independent creators to advertise and sell their services. At the last meetup Stan organized, startup founders jet-skied the East River at golden hour. At the incubator event, the entirety of which was filmed for use in a reality show that Stan plans to release sometime soon (though it is uploading Instagram clips daily), magnetic personalities were among the most valuable commodities. Stan cofounder Vitalii Dodonov told me that the 30 participating teams were chosen from a pool of 700 applicants, primarily for their existing social media followings and their ability to grow them. "It's not the building that gets you to revenue, it's the distribution," he said of today's startup culture. Of the many metrics competing teams were required to meet daily (10 sales calls, for example), social media videos were among the most heavily weighted. Everywhere I looked, people were talking about their companies into phones attached to tripods. Their products ran the gamut of usefulness — ranging from an AI facial scanner that tracks acne to an AI app that connects parents with babysitters. Dodonov and John Hu, Stan's other cofounder, were trailed at all times by multi-person film crews, who glared should you emit an ill-timed sound while the cameras rolled. (The Velcro rip of my messenger bag earned me some leers.) Even outfits were choreographed. On the advice of the camera crews, Hu wore a "cream" colored getup while Dodonov donned a "charcoal" number to emphasize what was described to me as the "yin and yang" paradigm between the two. I spent about 16 cumulative hours at the event over two days earlier this month, at Stan's invitation. I ate meals with the founders, did a 7:30 a.m. cold plunge in the on-site lake alongside a Danish guy selling an AI to-do list, and commiserated with the startup founders who routinely pulled all-nighters to hit their metrics. Here's what I learned from the experience. The event was billed as a sort of reality-TV-style game show-slash-incubator in the vein of hits like "Love Island" and "Squid Game." As in those shows, founder teams at Launchpad were subject to firepit eliminations, discreet alliances, and competitive drama under the ever-watchful lenses of dozens of expensive cameras. Except instead of a bunch of promiscuous co-eds doing risque challenges on a tropical island somewhere, contestants at Launchpad were mostly tech geeks with an unhealthy number of hours notched building software on their MacBooks. "There's no sex," laughed Jacob Snarr, a 24-year-old from Philadelphia. "Nobody here is thinking about that." Snarr and his cofounder, RJ McLaughlin, built a web browser game that lets friends debate their tastes and preferences, from their favorite foods to other everyday questions. The pair enlisted me as a product tester one morning, and we debated the merits of empanadas in the chilly barn. McLaughlin and Snarr were in second place on the leaderboard when I talked to them on Saturday morning — saving them from elimination. Rey Mendoza, who at 41 was one of the oldest founders in the competition, had already been eliminated. When I spoke with him, he was fighting for a chance at redemption. He showed me his sleep tracker for the six days. He hadn't slept more than six hours a night. "Here, you're just fucking building, like 24/7," Mendoza, fatigued, said reverently. Event organizers added a number of less-intense, more fun-oriented events to the schedule, which were largely ignored by teams scrambling to upload more videos to social media. A "Mario Kart" meetup in a room adjoining the cafeteria was attended by precisely nobody. Two TVs showed the game's start screen, while maybe a dozen people sat at tables squinting at laptops. It's hard to imagine binge-watching some 60 sweatshirt-clad nerds drearily prompting chatbots to refine source code for yet another quirky AI startup. After all, everyone and their cousin is vibe coding their way into progressively nicher business models these days. In 2025, a record number of business applications — about 5.7 million — were submitted by Americans, according to census data. However, the number of businesses the government estimates will be successful enough to require employees actually declined. Those kinds of numbers mean it takes more to stand out. In our interview, Hu pointed at my phone and said I could use AI tools to start three or four businesses today — but, of course, they likely wouldn't be profitable. That, Hu said, is where the founders' personalities are supposed to come in, together with a bit of manufactured drama and endless streams of social media content. In the first challenge of the event, held on the first day, for example, teams were required to submit one social media video for public review around the firepit. Then, in front of everyone, Hu tore into them. "I was very honest," he said of one particular "roast" that produced tears from the submitters. "I was like, 'Guys, would anyone ever watch this? No. The answer is no, because of the quality — you never have a shot." The moment would certainly make for good television. It also, Hu told me, mimicked the real-life struggle inherent in starting a company in a saturated market. "They're going through the true ups and downs of a true cofounder relationship and a startup experience," he said of the team that was subjected to his roast, who were initially so dejected they discussed "breaking up." Overall, most of the teams I talked to said they enjoyed the ramshackle experience of trying to make a company profitable in two weeks. At the very least, it was all happening in a picturesque setting. Stan spared no expense to pull off the event. It was held at a luxury, 400-acre villa two hours north of New York City that has in the past hosted retreats for high-flying companies like J.P. Morgan, whose executives, according to one staff member at the retreat at least, are keen for employees to embrace buzzwords like "team-building" and "company culture" among the illusion of rustic calm far from Manhattan. We were in the sticks of eastern Pennsylvania — so deep in the woods, in fact, that cell service was nonexistent. There was fiber-optic internet, however, and the setting, though far-flung, could hardly be called rustic. A squadron of golf carts staffed by the venue's seasonal workforce, many of whom were from Ireland or Australia, patrolled the grounds. I was personally given the cellphone number of one such seasonal worker and encouraged to notify her anytime I wanted to go anywhere, at which point she would materialize with the golf cart. Dodonov told me that Stan spent a combined $3 million renting the place for two weeks, booking camera crews, and making other necessary arrangements to host the founders, some of whom had traveled from as far away as Spain and Denmark. For a company whose cofounder told Business Insider this year that it has an annual recurring revenue of "nearly $41 million," that's a significant sum. "It's a very expensive experiment," Dodonov said. He said that, in his view, the return on investment is to see if "the playbook works" — the playbook being his and Hu's belief that building a successful company requires, perhaps above all, promoting yourself on social media. "You've never been on a cruise?" my friend basically yelled at me while we were planning an adults-only trip away from our kids. She insisted that cruising with her grandparents as an adult was one of the best trips she's ever taken. So, despite being a little terrified of being aboard essentially a floating skyscraper with thousands of people, I agreed to a Disney cruise for just the two of us. Honestly, it was so much fun that I'm already planning another Disney cruise with my kids — though I'm not sure I want to give up the adults-only version. My family is known for taking really elaborate vacations. One time we stayed on a remote island near Sicily, which is an active volcano. It took us three flights and a long ferry ride to get there, but it was totally worth it to see the lava at night. This trip was different. We took a flight from Boston to Orlando, boarded the Disney Wish, and after that, we didn't have to think about anything. We have seven kids between the two of us (including three sets of twins), and the ease of the Disney cruise was exactly what we both needed. There were activities nonstop, and you could join any of them at any point. I took a quick class to learn how to draw Ursula, we participated in so many trivia games with other adults, and stopped to take photos with characters — who are all over the boat all the time — to send home to our kids. Part of its ease was that most everything was included, so there were few extra costs. For example, all meals at the themed restaurants were part of the package, and we could order as many dishes as we wanted. Non-alcoholic beverages are also included, and you get room service 24/7. I especially liked the buffet-style meals at Marceline Market because I could mix in some healthy options (there were plenty) with some of my faves, like the fried hash browns for lunch or the Mickey-shaped churro waffles (which were highly recommended by the whole staff). Of course, there are fancier options, like the Italian restaurant Palo, for which we couldn't get a reservation during our trip. That said, we spent plenty of time at the Keg & Compass pub because on the first night I discovered their vodka dirty martini, which was hands down the best one I've ever had (yes, including fancy New York restaurants). Cocktail prices varied from bar to bar, but this martini was $14, which seemed super reasonable to me. Disney cruises in the Caribbean stop at Disney's private island, Castaway Cay. And for me, it was a key stop. While I've been on a lot of boats growing up — my dad loves fishing — I still get seasick a lot. And while I was surprised by how little the cruise ship rocked, I could still feel it a little bit. So getting off the boat and having my feet on the sand was necessary for me. I also love the ocean, and the Caribbean water is the perfect mix of temperature, color, and soft sand. My favorite moment was drinking a frozen piña colada with my friend while taking in some sunshine. I appreciated that the island has an adults-only section called Serenity Bay, which was quieter and more relaxed than the family beach. There's a restaurant off the beach, too, so we were able to eat lunch between dips in the water. While there were nonstop activities on the boat, I was often torn between wanting to do two or more overlapping things. For example, there was bingo one night happening at the same time as trivia. Given the option, I would've done both, because who doesn't love a bingo night? There was another day when you could make your own friendship bracelets, but I had already booked a facial, and that craft didn't repeat during our stay. Because our main goal was to spend time together and relax, I felt I didn't do many of the interesting activities the boat offered. But I also get that that's the point; there's something for everyone at any given time of the day. Being a newbie worked against me when booking extra activities. I wanted to surprise my friend with a couple's massage so we could destress, and I also wanted a facial. By the time I went to book spa treatments (about a week before we boarded), there were very few time slots available. Next time, as soon as I book my trip, I'll be adding all the extras I want to maximize availability. That said, we ended up getting our massage on embarkation day, which turned out to be the perfect way to smoothly transition from the chaos of mom life to vacation mode. And at $399 for both of us, it wasn't that much more expensive than the massages I get back in Maine. I booked my facial for 8 a.m., which felt a little early, but again was the only available time. If I were to do it again, I'd book the facial in the afternoon so as not to cut into pool time. When I tell you I packed and unpacked my bag about 10 times before boarding, I'm not exaggerating. The Disney cruise hosted a pirate night and a Halloween party, and I wanted to be prepared for both. I also didn't know what to expect to want to wear on a cruise, so I overpacked by a ton. This left me with very little room for souvenirs, which I still bought, but had to carry an extra tote bag back home. All the shops on the boat have different themes and therefore offer different stuff. I bought a Mickey-cruise-themed men's shirt that got so many compliments on the day I wore it. I also bought my kids pens and small keychain stuffies with their favorite characters. My friend, who has more cruise experience than I do, insisted it wouldn't be weird for us to be on a Disney cruise without kids. And she was right. We weren't the only ones enjoying the adults-only areas, which included an ample pool deck with a jacuzzi, a small pool, a dedicated bar, and a coffee shop. There were also adults-only activities, like dance parties and trivia. And obviously, all the bars were for 21+. While we only stayed at the adults-only pool deck, we could still hear the movies blasting for the family-friendly pool deck, which at times made it hard to relax. That said, when "Frozen" came on, both my friend and I were singing along (and probably annoying other adult guests). We met a couple who were older than us who were on their 41st cruise. They found me adorable, being so excited about my first experience on board. They told me to get ready to become a cruise person, and they weren't wrong. I had such a great time that I'm already planning when to take another Disney cruise, this time with my whole family. Disney Cruise Lines just announced a new ship called Believe, which will feature an "Encanto" stage show — which just happens to be my kids favorite Disney movie.  I cannot wait to see my kids' eyes go wide when they see how many things they can do, and for them to be ready to take a photo with their favorite Disney character, Daisy Duck. Trick-or-treating might cater to the gatherers of the world, but the full moon that falls just before Halloween is for the hunters. The Hunter's Moon will join millions of jack-o'-lanterns across America to light up the night sky on October 26, 2026, peaking just after midnight.  The moniker "Hunter's Moon" refers to the full moon that follows the Harvest Moon, which is the one that falls closest to the fall equinox. This mid-autumn moon goes by many names in different cultures, but its symbolic associations with introspection, preparation, completion, and clarity are universal. Â  The Hunter's Moon is to the Harvest Moon as meat is to potatoes. Equally important for seasonal nourishment, the Harvest Moon represents the traditional time for farmers' final crops, while the following full moon centers on acquiring meat ahead of the winter months. Moonlit fields that are cleared of crops and filled with plumped-up, pre-hibernation animals make for favorable hunting conditions. They were in fact so ideal that hunters regularly turned to the light of October's full moon to help them stock up on a whole winter's worth of meat for the family. While we can now turn to Costco for our seasonal hoarding needs, the deeply-rooted survival practice linked to the Hunter's Moon has made the name stick.  Like most other full moons, the Hunter's Moon goes by different monikers depending on who you talk to. In various Native American cultures, names for this moon reflect everything from harvest traditions to changing weather. The Dakota dub it the Drying Rice Moon in honor of rice preparations that take place prior to winter, while the Anishinaabe call it the Falling Leaves Moon for the crunchy, windswept leaves that color the air in autumn. The Ojibwe and Haida, meanwhile, know this full moon as the Freezing Moon or Ice Moon, and the Cree call it the Migrating Moon, a reference to southward-bound migratory birds. Other names for this moon are the Travel Moon, Dying Grass Moon, Blood Moon, and Sanguine Moon.  While the history of the Hunterâs Moon is all about stocking the pantry, the symbolic side is more about taking stock of your mindset. The month of October spans a full lunar cycle that marks the transition from harvest to preservation, culminating in the Hunterâs Moon.  Across different traditions, this time of year has long been marked by a shift in the air: in Celtic culture, this window brushes right up against Samhain, a time when the veil to the spiritual world is lowered, and communication with ancestors and spirits is enhanced. Similarly, across parts of India, this same lunar phase coincides with Sharad Purnima, a moonlit celebration of the closing of the monsoon season. A common ritual is to soak kheer, a type of rice pudding, under the light of the full moon and then eat it at dawn. Itâs the first full month of fall after the autumn equinox, providing a prime opportunity for internal reflection on the connections and feelings accumulated throughout the year. With winter comes a focus on preparing for the season aheadânot just in terms of getting and storing what we need, but also protecting the parts of your life that serve you and pruning those that don't. Think of it as a last sliver of light leading you to an entrance you can slip through before the door closes. In other words, itâs a nudge to stop putting things off. Whether that means finally having that tough conversation, walking away from a situation that has run its course, or simply dealing with the emotions you've been avoiding, itâs a true act of self-preservationâa chance to clear the air now instead of letting those unresolved things weigh you down all winter. The moon has many different faces, and with that, many ways to honor them. Because this phase is all about balancing decisiveness with deliberation, you can lean into whatever feels most grounding for you right now. Like a hunter, itâs important to observe your surroundings before deciding where to aim your energy. In a day-to-day sense, that can mean writing down your abundancesâand what might be dragging you downâto narrow in on what deserves your focus ahead of a lower-energy season. Full moons are naturally tied to release, making this an ideal time to drop what no longer serves you. Whether that means letting go of bad habits built up throughout the year or intense emotions that will only weigh you down in the season ahead, this is your chance to clear the slate. And amidst all that release and restock, like with any full moon, the Hunter's Moon is also a chance to practice gratitude. Under the bright light of the full moon, thank the universe for the abundance of the past harvest and anything that's serving you, and simply enjoy the beauty of the moon framed by the fall foliage. Login  Ro  18 October 2026   Apple iOS Versus Featured  We've got a new iPhone in town, but the age-old question remains: do I get the new iPhone, or is last year's model just as good? With the Apple iPhone 18 Pro now released, the Apple iPhone 17 Pro stock is running low as Apple has discontinued the model. However, if you act fast, you might find one that will feel just like the new iPhone, but at a lower price. After all, the upgrades this year are quite modest. Looking beyond the specs, the iPhone 18 Pro does promise some improvements in certain aspects, so let's take a closer look and try to find the nuances. For starters, you can compare the complete specs sheets or directly continue with our editor's assessment  in the following text. The previous iPhone generation was the one that introduced the new design language that will serve as a foundation for the upcoming generations, so it's no surprise that there are almost no changes to the appearance of the two phones. Even the dimensions are identical to the point where you can put a case from the old model on the new one. However, if you are not paying attention, it's easy to miss the new Dynamic Island, which is narrower than before and thus takes away less screen real estate. This allows Apple to squeeze in three ongoing activities in the Dynamic Island. Of course, there are new colors as well. The iPhone 18 Pro now comes in Black, Silver, Glacier and Burgundy, with the latter being the hero color this year. The 17 Pro, on the other hand, is offered in Silver, Cosmic Orange and Deep Blue. The newer iPhone Pro comes with the same exact 6.3-inch LTPO OLED display as its predecessor. Our tests confirm it, and the supported features confirm it. In either case, you are getting a bright, feature-packed display with anti-reflective properties. The iPhone 18 Pro offers negligible battery capacity increase over its predecessor, so we weren't expecting any endurance gains to begin with, but we were pleasantly surprised. The new Pro achieved better results in all of our screen-on tests and scored a higher Active Use Score as a result. Then again, one could argue that the battery life improvements are trivial at best. It's important to note that these tests were carried out on units with physical SIM card slots, meaning eSIM-only units will likely score a tad higher as they carry bigger batteries. In our experience, the difference is hardly a big one.  Apple advertised marginal charging speed improvements, and the results from our tests corroborate the company's claims. The iPhone 18 Pro seems to be only 2 percentage points faster at the 15-minute checkpoint and 4 percentage points faster at 30 minutes. Still, the new Pro pulls ahead in the last lap and crosses the finish line about 16 minutes faster. It's not much, but it's something. We are hard-pressed to find any meaningful changes to the overall tuning of the speakers in the newer model, so they sound just as great as before. But when it comes to loudness, the 18 Pro is considerably louder. Usually, when you increase the volume of tiny speakers like these, you get worse audio quality, but Apple managed to maintain the excellent output while improving loudness, so kudos for that. To be honest, the only generational-worthy upgrade that we got this year with the new iPhones is the chipset. The new Apple A20 Pro SoC appears to be considerably more powerful than the A19 Pro powering the iPhone 17 Pro. It's also based on a more efficient 2nm manufacturing process and employs twice as many Neural Engine cores responsible for AI-related tasks. Both iPhones ship with 12GB/256GB memory by default, but only the 18 Pro goes up to 2TB storage. The 17 Pro caps at 1TB.   Be aware, however, that independent testing has revealed that the 1TB and 2TB versions of the iPhone 18 Pro use QLC storage, which suffers a significant drop in write speeds once the storage is more than 60% full. Camera comparison Apple introduced a couple of reasonably significant hardware changes last year (new telephoto and new selfie camera), so the 18 Pros keep the upgrades to a minimum - the main camera gets a variable aperture lens which is also brighter at the wide open end compared to the one on the 17 Pros. The range is f/1.48 to f/4.0, with two in-between settings (f/1.8 and f/2.8). The 17 Pros' aperture is fixed at f/1.78. Teardowns revealed there's a new sensor model being used on the main camera, but it still has the same basic specs - 1/1.28" optical format and 48MP resolution. The camera uses sensor-shift image stabilization, as before. The telephoto camera remains the same as last year, with its 100mm equivalent lens providing 4x optical zoom, but the lack of close focusing remains a pain point. The ultrawide is around 13mm equivalent - again, unchanged. All these sensors have a 1/2.55" optical format and a 48MP nominal resolution. As last year, all three rear cameras offer 24MP shooting capability, and that's the default setting too - you get that at 0.5x, 1x, and 4x, while the 2x and 8x zoom levels stick to 12MP. At the native zoom levels, you also get a 48MP option. The selfie camera remains unchanged, too. Its squarish 18MP sensor provides enough image area to capture selfies in either portrait or landscape orientation, without having to rotate the phone itself. A new development this year that just might be the most important one, and the one actual significant difference between the 18 Pros and the 17 Pros, is the manual mode in disguise. You get the option to set shutter speed and white balance, in addition to the main camera's aperture, though manual ISO setting is still missing. It's not a dedicated mode and you kind of have to set each parameter separately from its own sub-menu from the contextual settings pane, but it's still something that the 17 Pros don't have. After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be releasing its first touchscreen MacBook as early as November 6th, after announcing it as early as October 27th. Of course, rumors are rumors – though essentially every reputable source has aligned on the idea of the MacBook Pro gaining support for touch very shortly. Apple even left a few hints in macOS 27: Touch Support in Sidecar, pull to refresh support, and slightly bigger menu bar items. One could call all of this a mere coincidence, but it’s probably exactly what it looks like. Regardless, here’s what the first touchscreen MacBook will have to offer. On the display panel side of things, the redesigned MacBook Pro will come with a Tandem OLED display. This will be similar to the iPad Pro, which is often touted as one of the best mobile displays on the market. Tandem OLED comprises of stacked OLED panels, which allows for incredible colors, strong contrast, and increased brightness. Reports also suggest it’ll come with a Dynamic Island, and it’ll be a bit smaller than the one on the iPhone. It won’t, however, come with support for Face ID. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple will have some special optimizations for the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, beyond what’s already visible in the betas of macOS 27: “For instance, if users touch a button or control, the interface will bring up a new type of menu surrounding their finger that provides more relevant options for touch commands. The software will also display the most appropriate set of controls based on users’ prior interaction. And if a person taps an item in the menu bar at the top of the screen, the set of controls will enlarge to be more easily selectable with a finger.” Despite initial reporting suggesting that we’ll be seeing the debut of the M6 Pro and Max in the redesigned MacBook Pro, Apple is now skipping the release of those chips to accelerate the M7. This means that the first iteration of 2nm chips won’t be making their way to the redesigned MacBook Pros, and they’ll instead offer the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. There won’t be a base model version of this computer quite yet, though rumors suggest that Apple will be launching a base version of the redesigned MacBook Pro with an M7 chip as early as next spring. One design rumor for the new MacBook Pro is the fact that it’ll be slightly slimmer and lighter – though it’s unclear how meaningful this will be. The last MacBook Pro iteration made the computers look and feel quite chunky, so a bit of progress here would likely be welcome – so long as it doesn’t come at the compromise of thermals. Bloomberg has also reported that these computers will be ‘significantly lighter,’ thanks to re-engineering of internal components. Seems odd that they’d release this m5 in October, then March-May release the M7 version. Certainly would make me not want to buy it. According to the Power On newsletter, Apple will potentially release these new MacBook Pro models on November 6th, making a straight four weeks of new Apple launches with iPhone Duo, HomePod mini 2, the new MacBook Pro, and HomeView + Apple TV 4K.  As of now, there’s no Apple release scheduled for November 6th, so it would make sense to be the new MacBook Pro: Now, I have a little more to share: Apple is planning to hold a “reset” at its retail stores on the evening of Thursday, Nov. 5, into Friday, Nov. 6, that implies new signage and products will be placed on store tables. Stablecoin issuer Circle CRCL$82.25·Market Closed is defending its business model as Coinbase, its largest distribution partner, backs a rival that aims to give businesses more income from stablecoin reserves. In a blog post on Friday, Chief Commercial Officer Kash Razzaghi wrote that Circle kept about 7 cents in net profit for each dollar in revenue made during the first half of 2026. The firm brought in about $1.4 billion, while distribution and transaction costs totaled $819 million. The post puts the figures at the center of a dispute over who gets the interest earned on assets backing stablecoins. Circle said the remaining $473 million covered compliance, liquidity and product development. That figure also included about $214 million in stock-based compensation and related costs. Coinbase is Circle’s largest USDC partner, but is also a backer of Open USD, along with Stripe and BlackRock. Open USD, unveiled in June, aims to let businesses mint and redeem stablecoins without fees, while passing off reserve income minus a management fee to participants. Circle's post did not name Open USD, whose OUSD token is now live, directly, and there are other competitors like the Paxos-led Global Dollar Network (USDG) that also share reserve income with participants. "The costs of redemption, compliance, and resilience don't disappear just because the issuer declined to pay them," Razzaghi wrote. Circle has also been working to secure additional distribution partners. In September, Binance bought a $100 million stake in the firm under a five-year deal that includes a fee tied to USDC held through Circle's wallet service. Circle said standard USDC redemptions remain free and "typically settle in up to two business days." Qualifying platform customers and payment flows through Circle Payments Network can now access near-real-time redemptions at no cost, it said. Bitcoin BTC$82,001.05 could reclaim $100,000 before year-end as institutional adoption and demand for hard assets overcome near-term economic uncertainty, according to crypto asset manager Bitwise, offering a more bullish outlook than traders who expect inflation and elevated interest rates to constrain gains. The forecasts highlight a divide over timing. Analysts see longer-term support from institutional investment, regulatory progress and concerns about government debt, but disagree on whether those forces can drive a breakout before the end of 2026. Ryan Rasmussen, head of research at Bitwise, expects bitcoin to emerge from the coming weeks’ uncertainty at a higher valuation. “We believe bitcoin ends the year higher, potentially above $100,000,” Rasmussen told CoinDesk. He identified three longer-term drivers: institutional buying through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and corporate purchases; demand for hard assets amid inflation, rising debt and currency debasement; and clearer regulation that reduces the perceived risk of owning crypto. “In our view, these tailwinds significantly outweigh the potential headwinds,” he said. Rasmussen nevertheless expects volatility around a possible late-October Federal Reserve rate increase and November’s U.S. midterm elections. A breakout would be difficult in that environment, he said, although the uncertainty could create an opportunity for investors to build positions. Adam Morgan McCarthy, head of research at LO:TECH, a London-based crypto trading and market data firm, is more cautious. His base case is an $85,000–$95,000 trading range into year-end. “Macro has gone against Bitcoin all year, with the Fed hiking in September and a December hike priced at roughly 75%,” McCarthy said. “This will continue to weigh on bitcoin.” The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September. Inflation figures released Oct. 14 complicated the outlook: consumer prices rose 0.6% from the previous month, while core prices increased 0.3%. Gasoline accounted for more than half of the headline increase. McCarthy said a return above $100,000 would require expectations for a December hike to give way to a pause, supported by easing oil prices and inflation. James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares, sees a similar tension between persistent inflation and weakening employment. Cooling prices would give the Fed more room to respond to labor-market weakness; further inflation pressure could keep policy restrictive and weigh on bitcoin. The world’s largest cryptocurrency was trading around $81,500 at publication time. Luca Invernizzi, senior derivatives trader at Laser Digital, Nomura’s crypto subsidiary, expects bitcoin to remain largely a macro trade into year-end, taking its direction from longer-dated Treasury yields. He described the rebound from summer lows as unconvincing, citing thin volumes, fading ETF inflows and slowing corporate buying. Positioning offers more encouragement. Leverage has largely been flushed out of bitcoin, with much of the speculative excess moving into altcoins, Invernizzi said. McCarthy also sees fewer crowded bullish positions that could unravel. Funding rates, payments between perpetual futures traders, are at or below zero, while August’s rally was driven by traders closing bearish bets rather than adding new bullish positions. That reduces the fuel for forced selling and leaves room for another squeeze higher. “A clean break above $90K for BTC could trigger another round of short covering,” Invernizzi said. With implied volatility back near its lows and options pricing still tilted toward downside protection, he sees upside calls as an attractive way to position for a rally without chasing bitcoin in the spot market. The broader industry’s recovery provides another source of optimism. In a research note to clients earlier this week authored by Peter Christiansen, Citi (C) said total crypto market capitalization rose from roughly $2.1 trillion to nearly $3 trillion during the third quarter. Institutional ETF flows turned positive, while activity across exchanges, stablecoins and digital asset infrastructure improved. The bank also sees investors increasingly looking beyond crypto prices toward businesses supporting tokenization, custody, stablecoins and settlement. Regulatory progress continues despite the Clarity Act’s failure to advance, Citi said. Butterfill cautioned that investment-product flows have since slowed following $11.1 billion of inflows since mid-July. He views that as uncertainty rather than deteriorating bitcoin fundamentals, but said sustained gains require renewed buying. Like Rasmussen, he sees concerns about government finances as a potential longer-term source of demand. Higher Treasury yields typically hurt bitcoin by tightening financial conditions, but that relationship could shift if investors increasingly interpret those yields as compensation for fiscal risk. “Our bias is towards higher prices over the medium term, but we would want to see the fiscal argument translate into sustained allocations before expecting a decisive breakout,” Butterfill said. Rasmussen is more confident those forces will translate into gains sooner. “Once the market churns through this period, we expect bitcoin to rerate significantly higher,” he said. This post surveys some concerning attacks on TEEs. The goal is to persuade you to re-consider how you deploy TEE-based applications, if you should deploy them at all.  Trusted hardware companies (Intel, AMD, etc.) mainly compete on performance, functionality and (one hopes) developer-friendliness. They may try to compete on security, but this is hard, in my opinion: there’s always someone else who can (mis)claim more security and such claims are hard to adjudicate by the market. Furthermore, the complexity of modern CPU architectures and the pervasiveness of side-channels makes TEE security claims tenuous. In any case, (some of) the TEE attacks follow below. Enclaves are meant to protect secrets and integrity of computation from the environment (e.g., host OS, or even the physical environment). But even if the enclave platform is secure, bugs in the code running in the enclave can lead to disaster. Many of these attacks impacted not only Intel SGX but other TEE platforms as well, like AMD SEV. You may say: “I don’t care; my threat model precludes physical attacks.” No it doesn’t, silly: your remote attestation verifier accepts a quote from any Intel CPU in good standing. And the attacker’s CPU is one of them. A break of one is a break of all, unless… Unless: you pin your verifier to only accept your own PCK certificates6, which implicitly excludes the attacker’s CPU. This works for so-called scalable SGX (the only flavor left) and requires you to carefully manage a PKI. So, effectively requires you to wield a footgun. Good luck! DoS is explicitly outside the threat model of SGX, TDX, SEV-SNP and Nitro (b.c. the host can simply refuse to schedule the enclave). So, here, we focus on liveness issues due to issues with the TEE platform itself. So many7$^,$8$^,$9$^,$10. In theory, there are ways to reduce the attack surface of trusted hardware. For example, see Sanctum11 from my group at MIT back in the day (shameless plug).  Unfortunately, in practice, these more principled designs tend to come with lower performance and/or less functionality. Don’t put valuable secrets in your TEEs, or they’re likely to become public, especially if physical attacks are in your threat model12. Emergency Backstory Newsletters 中文新闻 BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA TOK PISIN By Nicole Hegarty By Courtney Bembridge 7.30 Topic:Rental Housing Persistent low vacancy rates are pushing renters to find creative solutions.  (ABC News: Jack Fisher) Extended families and friends are teaming up to improve their chances of securing a rental property as tight supply forces prices higher, with experts warning the cohort is being left behind. For Perth renter Grady Toomath, sharing a home with his brother and another housemate has become a necessity rather than a lifestyle choice. "I've been living here since 2019. When we moved in, the rent was $315 a week; [after] our latest rent increase it's $760 a week," he said. Avi Khan says there has been a massive shift in how prospective renters apply for properties.  (ABC News: Chris Gillette ) That is a 141 per cent increase over seven years that comes as the rental market continues to tighten. Brisbane real estate agent Avi Khan said multigenerational families and friendship groups accounted for one in five rental applications to his agency. "The only choice that they have is they come together as a family unit or rent a property with their housemate, their flatmate, their friends, whoever it is. It's the massive shift that we're seeing," Mr Khan said. Grady Toomath's living arrangement has stretched his budget a little further, but it has come with sacrifices. Grady Toomath lives with his brother and a housemate in Perth.  (ABC News) "Three guys in a pretty small space, we've had to really adjust," he said. "It's not entirely the lifestyle any of us wanted, but it's the lifestyle we can afford. So we help each other; we do what we can. "We work together in this small space and try to just mind each other and be respectful in the way we can, but it's not what any of us really envisioned for our lives." Mr Khan said the increase in group applications coincided with negative gearing and capital gains tax changes in May's federal budget, which had eaten away at supply. The median weekly rent for a house in a capital city is now $700. (ABC News: Jack Fisher) "They [the government] haven't considered the effect these changes will have downstream. So there's no one replacing those investors. "That's why we're seeing real warning signs in the economy at the moment because where do these tenants go? They've got no other choices." 7.30 has contacted the Federal Housing Minister for comment. Federal and state governments offer several incentives to assist buyers to purchase their first home, including the Albanese government's expanded 5 per cent deposit scheme. But Lyndall Bryant, a senior lecturer in property economics at Queensland University of Technology, said renters have been overlooked. According to Domain, the national rental vacancy rate was at 1 per cent in the September quarter, with just one in 100 properties available to lease. The federal budget's negative gearing and capital gains tax changes have dampened investment in the property market. (AAP: Mick Tsikas) Capitals outside Sydney and Melbourne experienced more severe supply shortages. Agents and property economists said that has pushed the 31 per cent of Australians who rent to be more creative. Topic:Housing Policy Topic:Housing Policy Analysis by Michael Janda Topic:Real Estate Industry Topic:Housing Policy "We've been seeing a lot of conversation about how to make housing more affordable for people who have a mortgage or are trying to buy," Dr Bryant said. Lyndall Bryant. (ABC News: Chris Gillette ) "We've seen billions of dollars put into social housing and community housing, but social and community housing is only between 3 and 5 per cent of our total housing stock. "In rough numbers, 25 per cent of all of our people who need housing are renters that rent into the private market. There just isn't enough stock for them." The federal government increased Commonwealth Rental Assistance payments in 2023 and 2024 and has agreed, along with state and territory first ministers, to move toward more nationally consistent rental rights. Unions and housing advocacy groups have also called for rental caps and multi-year lease agreements. The national rental vacancy rate was 1 per cent in the September quarter. (ABC News: Keana Naughton) But Dr Bryant said the federal budget's tax changes have discouraged investment in housing, disadvantaging renters. "Our current policy arrangement is that it's dis-incentivising investors from being in residential property and we don't have enough landlords, and they're exiting the market," she said. "[It's] freeing up housing for first home buyers, which is really wonderful for first home buyers, but we still have this really large portion of the market that are renters and their prices are only going up." Sydney accountant Keegan Du Preez has nine investment properties across the country but also rents. The 24-year-old said he appreciated the challenges of the market from both the landlord and tenant perspective. "I try and look after the tenant. It's in my best interest, plus it's in the tenant's best interest as well to lock in that rate because the market's only going to go up with rents," he said. "So them locking in for 24 months helps them budget far better than if you have an increase every 12 months." Sydney accountant Keegan Du Preez is a rentvestor with nine investment properties. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard) He said rent increases were a last resort, but property owners needed to cover expenses. "Interest rates have spiked significantly; repair costs have gone up. Tradies, there's just a lack thereof, so all the tradies have put their prices up. So you have to compensate somewhere," he said. "As landlords, we're not an endless pit of money. "If it means that I go without for a month or two or three in order to look after my tenants, so be it. "If that is what's required to make sure that the portfolio plus the tenants [are] looked after, that is a sacrifice that landlords sign up [for] the very first day that they buy the property as an investor." Point your phone at a tall building and snap a photo, then look at it. The whole thing is leaning back like it’s trying to dodge a punch, and that effect has a name: converging verticals. Architecture photographers have spent about a century fighting it with view cameras and shift lenses, which tend to be heavy, pricey, or both. Lachlan Fysh, a Melbourne designer with a serious building habit, decided to fight it with a 3D printer, a CNC machine, and a wooden dowel. The result is the FTC-1, a 6×7 film camera that just took Gold for Cameras at the 2025 International Design Awards. The FTC-1 shoots 120 film on Mamiya RB67 backs and borrows lenses from the large format world, whose oversized image circles leave plenty of room to move. Turn a knob and the lens rises up to 30mm (1.2 inches), keeping the camera perfectly level while the frame slides up to catch the top of the tower. A second mechanism handles 15mm (0.6 inches) of sideways shift, and the back spins between portrait and landscape on magnetic detents. The whole package weighs 2.4 pounds (1.1 kg) and sells for $1,200 AUD, roughly $850. The Swiss cameras that pull off the same trick start in the thousands before you’ve even bought a lens. Designer: Lachlan Fysh (Fysh Technical)        Fysh’s first prototype was printed entirely in plastic, and it worked surprisingly well until he put it on a tripod. The body would sway for a beat after every adjustment before settling down, which is a dealbreaker on a camera you focus by squinting at ground glass. Over coffee in Japan, Oscar Oweson of Panomicron, who builds his own indie cameras, nudged him toward aluminum. Fysh brought in CNC-machined aluminum plates for the core and tripod base, where stiffness actually matters. Everything that just needs to hold its shape stayed printed, keeping the body light enough for a guy who still shoots from a bicycle. Machining the FTC-1’s big hollow lens cones from solid metal would leave a mountain of aluminum shavings on the floor, which Fysh disliked on environmental grounds. Printing them uses a fraction of the material and still delivers all the stiffness they need. Because he runs FDM printers at home, he can print a cone to order for whatever lens you own, and reprint one fast if you pick the wrong size. The ring-shaped brackets holding the handle would be a nightmare to mill, so those are 3D printed metal, now titanium for a little weight saving. Even the ground glass is acrylic, which stays flat, survives being dropped, and keeps the price down.        The rise mechanism runs on a TR8 lead screw, the same 8mm threaded rod that drives the vertical axis on loads of desktop 3D printers. Fysh started with smaller TR4 and TR5 screws to save weight, but they forced a choice between slow adjustment and reliable locking. A lead screw only holds its position on its own when its lead stays under roughly 60% of its diameter, so a speedy 4mm lead needed the chunkier 8mm rod. Now the lens moves quickly and stays exactly where you leave it, with no separate locking knob. Earlier prototypes used rack and pinion gears, and Fysh admits he kept forgetting to tighten those. The brass part with the spring is an anti-backlash nut, and it’s the reason the rise feels so immediate. It’s essentially a nut split in two, with a spring pushing the halves against opposite sides of the thread so there’s zero slop when you change direction. Because TR8 hardware is everywhere in the 3D printing world, these nuts come off the shelf instead of being custom machined, which keeps costs sane. One Reddit commenter called the whole setup overkill, and Fysh is pretty confident it isn’t. I’m with Fysh here, since a buttery, slop-free rise is exactly what you want when nudging a frame by a millimeter on a windy rooftop.  Most technical cameras offer tilt, which angles the plane of focus (the Scheimpflug principle) so a landscape can stay sharp from the rock at your feet to the mountains on the horizon. Fysh left it out of the body on purpose. He worried that with a tilt mechanism built in, he’d never be totally sure it was sitting at zero, which is where he wants it about 95% of the time. His fix is a set of lens cones with a fixed tilt angle baked in, calculated for each focal length using a Scheimpflug visualizer he built himself. Swapping cones takes about a minute in the field, and the angle can never drift. The FTC-1 sells for $1,200 AUD (roughly $850) on the Fysh Technical site, with fixed tilt cones at $50 AUD each. Alpa’s 12 STC body alone costs CHF 4,300, north of $5,000, for similar rise and shift. Fysh builds each camera around a full-time job, so stock arrives in small batches, and a 6×17 panoramic sibling called the FTC-W is already in development on the same cone system. IDA’s global jury judges concepts and finished products alike, which makes this Gold sweeter, since you can actually buy the thing. Turns out the cure for converging verticals was a bike trip, a shed full of printers, and a guy stubborn enough to do the math. Gaza residents report rising prices after commercial shipments stopped, while families unable to afford extra supplies fear further shortages if the closure continues. Save Share Gaza City, Gaza — Prices of basic goods are rising rapidly in Gaza, where Israeli restrictions on the import of commercial goods are in their fifth consecutive day. Families already suffering from the siege on the enclave have started stocking up on goods they can still find, for fear of imminent shortages and continued price increases. The cost of flour, eggs, onions and other staples has sharply increased since Wednesday, when Israel said that commercial goods would no longer enter Gaza. This comes amid a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas, which still has some authority in the strip. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. The price of basic goods has soared, as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege. Residents without the means to buy in bulk will have to continue to purchase food when they can. They will be worst hit by the daily price rises if the border remains closed. The impact of the Israeli import restrictions is playing out in marketplaces, which are slightly busier than usual. Ismail al-Barawi, 52, from Jabalia in northern Gaza, noticed a significant rise in prices within two or three days of the crossings being closed on Wednesday. He described a recurring cycle of uncertainty in Gaza over the status of the crossings, which is usually followed by higher prices. Al-Barawi said a carton of eggs that had cost 35 shekels ($11.34) was now selling for between 60 and 70 shekels ($18 to $21). The price of a kilogramme of onions had risen from five or six shekels ($1.50–$1.80) to between eight and 10 shekels ($2.40–$3), while a kilogramme of avocados had increased from seven or eight shekels ($2.10–$2.40) to around 15 shekels ($4.50). “These increases happened in just two or three days,” he said, voicing concern about what prices would be if the crossings remain closed for another 10 to 15 days. The increases have forced him to buy smaller quantities of what he needs. Instead of a full carton of 30 eggs, he might buy only four or five. “Today, everyone is trading at the expense of the people. There is no mercy,” he said. He expressed frustration at traders, saying they raise prices as soon as they hear that crossings may remain closed, adding to the problem of real shortages. Al-Barawi predicted that a 50 kg sack of flour could end up costing 200 or even 300 shekels ($60–$90), if the crossings remained closed. Al-Barawi is responsible for providing food to his extended family of about 11 or 12 people, including his married daughters and their children. Whenever he has money, he prioritises basic goods such as flour, rice, cooking oil, onions and potatoes. Given the uncertainty, it makes sense for Palestinians to stock up now before prices increase further. But many families in Gaza have no money to spare, he added. “Some people cannot even afford to feed themselves for a day. How much can they save or store when they have no money?” he said. But stockpiling also has its limits. Fresh vegetables can spoil within days, he said. Unreliable electricity supplies make it difficult to store meat for more than a brief period. Gaza’s Government Media Office on Thursday rejected Israel’s explanation for the suspension, denying that authorities in the territory had imposed taxes or government fees on commercial trucks. The office said the 10,000-shekel ($3,242) amount cited by Israel was linked to a voluntary community fund intended to support vulnerable families and financial relief projects. It also said measures requiring a 30 percent rate for cash transactions had been introduced in agreement with the Chamber of Commerce to address a shortage of cash liquidity and the circulation of worn-out banknotes. The office accused Israel of using the dispute to impose further restrictions on supplies entering Gaza, which has been under an Israeli blockade since 2007. Gaza authorities were not to blame for the reduction of trucks entering the enclave, it said, and called on mediators and international parties to push for the entry of 600 trucks a day, in line with existing agreements with Israel. The office warned that continued restrictions would worsen the humanitarian and economic crisis in Gaza. Food remains unaffordable for many households in Gaza. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that food prices in Gaza in September 2026 averaged 204 percent above pre-October 2023 levels, when the genocidal war on Gaza began and Israel tightened restrictions on goods entering the enclave. OCHA’s October 2 situation report, before the new border restrictions were imposed, documented the wider humanitarian pressures facing residents. Iman Atallah, a 50-year-old displaced woman living in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, said the suspension of food deliveries has brought back memories of the man-made famine which hit the enclave in 2025. Atallah said the price of a sack of flour had already risen from between 25 and 35 shekels ($7.50–$10.50) before the closure to about 80 shekels ($24). With little income and a family to support, she said that even buying basic food had become increasingly difficult. “Before the crossings closed, flour was affordable. We could somehow manage to buy it. Now it costs 80 shekels ($24),” she said. The flour her family receives through aid distributions lasts less than a month. Fresh fruit and eggs are not completely unaffordable. “We used to eat more, and we could buy eggs for the children. Now we’ve had to give those things up,” she said. Her family now relies on rice and lentils, and they can afford only a little bread. Atallah said they sometimes skip breakfast or dinner, with lunch as their main meal of the day. Atallah’s family is one of the many in Gaza unable to afford extra supplies and facing a bleak outlook if the crisis continues. “We cannot stock up because we have no income,” she said. “If the crossings remain closed for 10 or 15 days, everything will become extremely expensive. Those who have money will stock up, while those who do not will just have to watch.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Your audio source don't have to take turns Now Playing Card is a GNOME Shell extension that shows track info and playback controls for every audio app and media tab open, all in one place – the panel or the Quick Settings menu. GNOME’s default media controller (and the many now playing applets and add-ons I’ve written about in the past) is fine for what you’re playing at the time, but less good if you juggle multiple audio apps during your day.  With Now Playing Card, pausing one thing to start playing another doesn’t mean it vanishes. So the podcast and Spotify track you paused mid-way through to check out a YouTube video in your browser? They stick around, ready to resume. Now Playing Card uses ‘cards’ for each player, with album art (size can be changed), player icon and a functional progress bar you can click on to seek (if the player supports it). Plus, playback controls, including loop and shuffle (where available). Since multiple players being on pause could take up a lot of room in the applet, the extension uses an ‘accordion’ effect to make best use of space. Only one player card is enlarged at a time, the rest being compact until clicked.  It can also show the actively-plating track name, artist and control buttons on the panel too, which is the main use-case for these things (“what’s this track” – look up and see). You can choose the position, size, behaviour, etc of those via the extension’s settings. Adding a bit of visual flourish to the label is an animated sound wave icon or, if you want to dial up the bling, a spectrum analyser with bars reacting to audio in real time. Mercifully, you can opt for no animated tic at all, if you’d rather.  A slew of visual customisation and behavioural settings are offered. Now Playing Card hides GNOME’s stock media controller in the notification/calendar pop-over (never sure what most people call it) when active. I do find that applet text scaling is a little “off” compared to other applets I open, but perhaps  accommodate multiple players – it can show up to 10 at a time – it kind of has to be smaller than standard to fit ’em in. Not everything that plays audio and reports over MPRIS is something you might care about (browser auto-play videos, looking at you) so there is “ignore” list in settings to help you keep your card list from getting too noisy. Want to try it? Now Playing Card is compatible with GNOME 45 to 51, which means if you’r reading from Ubuntu 24.04 LTS through to 26.10 you’re good to go. The film‘s grosses were strong, with “La Bola Negra” earning $277,500 from just four venues in New York and Los Angeles, for a per-screen average of $69,375. It’s the second-highest per-screen average for a Non-English language film of all time. But more importantly the film also makes history, becoming the first Netflix release to ever publicly disclose box office grosses. That marks a shift in strategy for the streamer, which has released films in theaters exclusively for several weeks to qualify for Oscars, but has been dodgy about the money they’re actually making. It briefly pulled back the curtain on the results for “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery,” but never officially. But it’s a new dawn, it’s a new day for Netflix, which will start to report box office results like the rest of its studio and streaming brethren.             Related Stories How Titmouse Animation Gave ‘Street Fighter’ Its Secret Sauce ‘You Can See Everything’ Opens to a Staggering $15 Million, Securing A24’s Place as Hollywood’s Hottest Brand  So get ready for headlines about how David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” Taika Waititi’s animated feature “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory,” Peter Berg’s “The Mosquito Bowl,” and Danny Boyle’s “Ink” fare when they open in theaters. All will have theatrical windows of roughly a month or more, which will give them access to more screens. But will Netflix enjoy the scrutiny? Apple sure seemed to hate it, discovering it was great to report box office when you had the goods (“F1”) and not so hot when you did not (“Fly Me to the Moon,” “Argylle”).             But Netflix has bigger problems at the moment. Its stock is in a rut and it has just enacted a punishing wave of layoffs, pink-slipping 1,000 employees and jettisoning Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria in favor of Fox and Disney vet Peter Rice. Will an embrace of traditional theatrical releases provide Netflix with an invaluable new source of revenue or will Wall Street treat box office grosses as another metric to pummel Ted Sarandos with when it finds them lacking?  So far, Netflix seems happy with the results. The streamer noted that “La Bola Negra’s” look at gay history appealed to younger audiences, the same ones driving the box office rebound. To that end, 51% of its opening weekend crowd was under the age of 35, with ticket buyers between 25 to 34 making up the largest age group at 39%. “La Bola Negra,” which Netflix picked up at Cannes for around $5 million, may be important in another key way. Awards voters seem to be embracing it and there’s a chance that it could overcome “The Odyssey” to land Netflix the Best Picture Oscar it has long coveted. Microsoft's positioning on physical games is still unclear ... but this latest job vacancy might offer a hint. What's going on?  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Microsoft might be planning to take a sharp left turn on the whole digital games argument, with this new Xbox job vacancy. The summer has been quite fractious for the gaming industry. Xbox has laid off hundreds and divested, closed down studios. And Sony nuked all the good will it has built up over the years by announcing PlayStation will no longer support physical discs, while reiterating in court testimony that it doesn't consider purchases to represent true ownership. Xbox has pulled in the opposite direction so far, in some ways. Xbox's new Disc-to-Digital program gives disc-based game owners digital rights simply for inserting the game into a compatible Xbox One or Xbox Series X console. But, Microsoft alone can't really stop the tide. It remains true that the only mass-market use case for Blu-ray drives these days are video game consoles, and if PlayStation is pulling out, the supply chain generally won't be viable at scale. Disc drive manufacturers are pivoting their assembly lines to adjacent industries, like lenses and lasers, ditching mechanical disc drives and putting disc-based games on notice. But, could there be an alternative? Microsoft is hiring a Xbox Games Supply Strategist. The primary responsibilities of this role include overseeing the launch of physical Xbox game releases, managing their global distribution strategy, inventory planning, sales execution, and retail channel operations. It appears that Xbox intends to continue supporting physical game releases in future generations as part of its broader gaming business strategy. https://t.co/SEBkdWafZOOctober 17, 2026 Users on X noticed last night that Microsoft has posted a vacancy for a "Xbox Games Supply Strategist" specifically focused on physical games. "The Xbox Games Supply Strategist will coordinate the launch of physical Xbox games across all platforms, lead development & oversee execution of global supply positioning strategies across all stages of the product lifecycle, ensure that inventory is positioned to deliver working capital/cost/service goals, and oversee the sales & channel execution of those games. You’ll work closely with Product Marketing, Finance & various groups within Supply Chain to establish & manage supply and sales plan of record. Every day will bring a new challenge, and you’ll be continually looking for ways to drive business profitability by planning and executing a predictable, reliable & low-cost supply chain." Notice that the copy makes no mention of discs here specifically ... Indeed, with disc drives for laptops, Blu-ray players, and even CD players being phased out, it doesn't seem entirely likely to me that Xbox Helix will have a traditional disc drive. But, it increasingly seems like Microsoft may be looking at alternatives. The Nintendo Switch range for example uses SD cartridges to deliver game licenses, and in some cases entire games when the speed is adequate. Could Microsoft be looking to follow suit here?      Microsoft has stayed fully quiet on its plans for physical games, even as PlayStation leaps head-first into self-imposed brand damage by telling users it's going all-in on digital. Digital-based games are the norm now, owing to convenience and often times price. Xbox Game Pass delivers hundreds of games for a low monthly fee, all digital. Steam accelerated the death of disc-based games on PC, and the Steam sales, cloud saves, and family sharing, and offline playback have become the gold standard for a digital games platform. Mobile games too have converted entire generations to assume gaming is a digital-first medium. Yet, in the core gaming audience, the hobbyist audience that makes up Xbox, Nintendo, and PlayStation's bulk customers — perhaps there's an opportunity for Microsoft here with Xbox Helix. Retail presence, physicality, that sense of ownership, and resale viability are all hugely popular aspects of the hobby. Microsoft would score a huge win with large swaths of the most passionate fans were it to announce long-term support for physical games delivery. But, Microsoft would also be swimming hard against the tide. The quiet majority has signalled pretty loud and clear they prefer digital, whether it's via Netflix, YouTube, Spotify, or gaming itself. But ... vinyl, 4K Blu-Ray, and even music cassettes have fought back in recent years, as discussions about ownership heats up. Perhaps Xbox could do something similar to Nintendo with Helix, delivering games via cartridges. Perhaps they could come up with something alternative, low cost and proprietary, even if it was just discs. Perhaps they could revive Skylanders toys and put game licenses on NFC chips inside action figures. Who knows? I guess we'll have to wait and see what Microsoft's ultimate play here is.
