Sense and Sensibility was Jane Austenâs debut novel, published anonymously in three volumes in 1811. Although she had been writing since childhood, Austen was 35 years old when the novel was released; she would publish three more in her lifetime (Pride and Prejudice in 1813, Mansfield Park in 1814, and Emma in 1815) before she died in 1817, at the age of just 41.  Her final two novels, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion, were published posthumously the same year.Â  Austen initially began writing Sense and Sensibility in 1795. Originally, she had written it with the title Elinor and Marianne (the name of the two sisters around whom much of the novelâs action takes place), and it was originally an epistolary novel (i.e., written in the form of postal letters). After more than a decadeâs work, she then hugely revised the manuscript in 1809, swapping out the letter-writing structure for a more narrative form, before looking to have it published soon afterward. Working with her brother Henry, who essentially acted as her agent, Austen submitted the novel to publisher Thomas Egerton. But in a move that was not uncommon at the time, she published the book on a commission basis and so took on a considerable financial burden in the publishing process herself. In accordance with the deal she worked out with Egerton, she would cover the production and advertising costs, while paying Egerton a commission to distribute the book to sellers. Whatever profits were left over were ultimately hers.Â  The commission arrangement was a risk, but happily the book sold well and, with the first print run selling out inside two years, eventually made a tidy profit. âYou will be glad to hear that every copy of [Sense and Sensibility] is sold and that it has brought me Â£140,â she wrote in a letter to her brother Frank in 1813. The book was clearly popular with readers (enough to warrant a second edition in the autumn of 1813) among whom was none other than Princess Charlotte Augusta, the 15-year-old daughter of the Prince Regent, and the future King George IV. âI have just finished reading [Sense and Sensibility],â Charlotte wrote in January 1812. âIt is certainly interesting, [and] you feel quite one of the company â¦ I must say it interested me much.â The young princess even went so far as to consider herself and the character of Marianne as being âvery like in disposition.âÂ Â  But contemporary critics found much to praise in Austenâs novel too. Although Austenâs novels all received only a handful of reviews in total, at least one anonymous review in the British cultural publication The Critical Review in 1812 called Sense and Sensibility âhighly pleasing,â and âjust long enough to interest the reader without fatiguing.â Supporting quotes and extracts were supplied for readers to make up their own mind, but on the whole the review stated that the âincidents are probable, and highly pleasing and interesting.âÂ  As was apparently a theme among critics and literary thinkers at the time, however, some early reviews also thought it important to not only discuss the novelâs literary merits, but its educational purpose as essentially a moral guidebook for young women too. As a result, the novel was commended for the many âbenefitsâ that female readers in particular will get from reading âthese volumesââwhile another anonymous write-up in The Critical Review in 1812 added that, âthe object of the work is to represent the effects on the conduct of life,â and in that sense it contains, âmany sober and salutary maximsâ alongside its âvery pleasing and entertaining narrative.â Not everyone was quite so convinced, however. One of only a handful of non-journalistic contemporary opinions came from Lady Henrietta Ponsonby, the wife of the English nobleman the Earl of Bessborough. Although she admitted that she found the book overall âamusingâ in a letter recommending the novel to a friend, Lady Bessborough also stated that âit ends stupidly.âÂ  Happily, most Austen fans today would likely disagree with her. Ram-pant costs. The PS6's memory and storage reportedly cost more than $680 between them. That's according to leaker Kepler_L2, who wrote that "RAM + NAND alone is over $680" in a NeoGAF thread in which Kepler_L2 was replying to a forum user who doubted an earlier cost estimate and suggested Sony could subsidise the PS6 to launch at $680. In June, insider Kepler_L2 - who has previously made claims about hardware that have turned out to be true - claimed the console's bill of materials had climbed to close to $1,000, up from their earlier estimate of around $760. It follows Sony Interactive Entertainment boss Hideaki Nishino telling investors in June that "as a principle, we do not intend to sell hardware at significant losses". Kepler_L2 didn't say how they arrived at the figure, and Sony has not, of course, confirmed any PS6 specs or pricing. We already know that console manufacturing is being heavily impacted by the ongoing component shortage, driven by the proliferation of AI datacenters, the war in Iran, and accusations of price fixing. It's therefore possible that we'll have to wait a while for Sony's next console - a console that is very likely to ship without support for discs and go all-in on Sony's controversial 'all-digital future'. Despite plenty of consumer outcry, the company has remained bullish in its commitment to scrapping discs by 2028 (the earliest, at this point, we're realistically going to see the PS6 on the market). It's also likely that Sony is going to push harder into subscriptions and cross-generational games. © 2026 Eurogamer.net a brand of IGN Entertainment, Inc. Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC. The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations. The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since. Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs. "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove. "In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter." Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly Â£21,000 cut from a typically valued home.  Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price. The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023. Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed. With mortgage rates at a three-year high, Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable. So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed. September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year. Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price. The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell. Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Rightmove. 'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak? You need Â£17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England. One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier."  Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home". But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget. Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial. "That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said. Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price. "The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said. But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it. In Scotland, the Home Report system, external requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market. Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain. His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London. He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England. The prediction market industry enables people to bet on US ‌elections and sporting events. Most Americans polled by Reuters/Ipsos are opposed to betting on US elections and other government actions. The prediction market industry, led by Polymarket and Kalshi, enables people to bet on US ‌elections, government policy moves and sporting events, which has resulted in a series of lawsuits involving state and federal agencies over who has the authority to regulate these markets. Some 69% of Democrats ​and 61% of Republicans polled said they opposed using prediction markets to bet on election results. The Reuters/Ipsos survey of 4,506 adults nationwide was taken on Sept. 30-Oct. 5. President ​Donald Trump’s administration is pursuing federal regulations for the industry through the CFTC, some of which are begin challenged in court by several states. Many expect ​the dispute to reach the US Supreme ⁠Court. The firm estimates robot-industry DRAM demand will rise from roughly 8,300 terabits this year to approximately 172,000 terabits by 2030 [1][2]. Counterpoint also projects that average DRAM capacity per humanoid robot will roughly double over the same period, from 19 gigabytes to 39 gigabytes [3]. The forecast positions physical AI â artificial intelligence deployed in machines outside data centers â as a potential new source of memory demand, according to the research firm. The note attributes the projected increase to more sophisticated AI models, which carry larger memory requirements. Counterpoint said humanoid robots process images, video and sound simultaneously and use "world models" to anticipate changes in the surrounding environment, requiring faster processing and greater memory capacity [3]. That assessment contrasts with warnings from major memory manufacturers, who continue to signal tight conditions through next year [3]. Goldman analysts said they are looking to Samsung's Oct. 29 earnings report for indications of whether the company expects tight memory-market conditions to persist in 2028 [3]. The global market is now projected to reach approximately 890,000 units by 2030 and 6.5 million units by 2035 (representing a $138 billion market opportunity)" [3]. Global memory firms are eyeing the robot market, according to the report [3]. Estimates of the economic scale involved vary widely; earlier commentary on the robot segment projected a possible market bifurcation between lower-cost Chinese robots and higher-cost American platforms [7]. The capital intensity of the underlying supply chain remains substantial, with Micron having expanded its U.S. investment to $200 billion, including $150 billion for manufacturing and $50 billion for research and development [8].Supply Response and Outlook Major memory giants continue to warn of tight conditions through next year, while CXMT's supply is coming online, according to company statements and analyst notes [3]. The tight-memory narrative may be tested after Samsung's earnings call, Goldman analysts said [3]. Counterpoint's forecast indicates DRAM demand could surge beyond data centers as humanoid robot deliveries are expected to begin next year and continue through the decade [3]. Memory demand will likely also rise for highly autonomous vehicles, which typically require over 200 GB of memory and several terabytes of storage, according to Micron's CEO [3]. Supply-side developments remain uneven. Micron broke ground on a Â¥1.5 trillion ($9.3 billion) expansion of its Higashihiroshima, Japan, factory, with high-bandwidth memory shipments expected to begin around the summer of 2028 [9]. CXMT's emergence as a large domestic DRAM producer â alongside Chinese NAND maker YMTC â has introduced new competitive pressure on the established suppliers, according to industry reporting [10].Conclusion Goldman has raised its humanoid robot shipment forecast to 890,000 units by 2030 and 6.5 million by 2035, citing a $138 billion market opportunity [3]. Memory makers and analysts are awaiting Samsung's Oct. 29 earnings report for signals on whether tight market conditions will persist, according to Goldman [3]. Acer's CEO has said chip prices could begin falling in the second half of next year [3]. The outlook depends on supply additions such as CXMT's mass production and the pace of humanoid robot deliveries [3]. By Anthony D'Alessandro  Editorial Director/Box Office Editor  	With the Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes documentary craze currently a stateside thing, Paramount/Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter was the ringleader at the worldwide weekend B.O. with a $51.1M global opening. Of that $20.1M came from 65 markets with the lionshare stateside with $31M.   	Again, this is several kicks up from what Street Fighter did in its last big-screen appearance with Jean- Claude Van Damme in 1994, that pic opening to $6.8M domestic, and ending its run at $33.4M stateside, and $99.4M global (all unadjusted for inflation and currency swings).   	Though Street Figther‘s opening round is lower than expected (a $70M worldwide opening was hoped for), I understand that this $82M net production will be fine in the end after all ancillaries per those in the know. For the Skydance owned Paramount, this is a distribution deal. Capcom and Legendary co-funded the movie. It was essentially the older fans who showed up and nobody else. Also, with a PG-13 rating, the hope is that an expanded family audience would come out for Street Fighter in a way that they couldn’t for the R-rated Mortal Kombat, based on another Gen X videogame.   	The reported opening on Mortal Kombat II was $63M WW with $23M from 78 territories on 31K screens. In like-for-likes, Street Fighter‘s foreign start of $20.1M is 4% ahead of Mortal Kombat 2 and 2% ahead of Free Guy.   Street Fighter was shot for Imax, which did $7.7M in its global network; broken out that’s $5.4M in North America (18% of the weekend) and $2.3M from 471 screens offshore.   	The No. 1 openings were in UK ($3.3M at 593 sites), Mexico ($1.8M at 865 sites), Australia ($1.6M at 260 locations), Panama ($228K) and Taiwan ($235K at 90 locations) and Indonesia with $384K at 480 theaters.   	No. 2s were Brazil ($1.2M at 726 locations), Malaysia ($491K at 138 locations), Hong Kong ($201K at 55 sites), Thailand ($200K at 257 locations) as well as UAE with $705K at 58 locations. Overall, the total Middle East region grossed $1.4M.  	           	The Kitao Sakurai directed movie was No. 3 in Germany ($850K at 436 theaters), Philippines with $275K at 206 theaters, and Colombia with $227K.  	The raging riots against the police curbed moviegoing in France where Street Fighter was No. 4 with $1.1M at 355 locations. Spain was also 4th with $550K at 298 locations in addition to Netherlands with $314K at 86 locales.   	In Japan, Street Fighter was the second MPA title in the market with $875K at 333 locations for a No. 5 rank. Also, the movie swung low in Italy with $451K at 250 locations. Korea didn’t have a front seat to the movie with a No. 8 $242K opening at 435 locations. Meanwhile in India, Street Fighter did $431K at 1,064 locations; that’s where the Nelson Dilipkumar directed action title Jailer 2 reigned with an estimated $18M (and global around $32M for a No. 2 rank). We’ll have more official figures on Jailer 2 from Rentrak later.   	Austin Abrams is more popular in his Sony/Constantin movie Resident Evil than Disney/20th Century Studio’s Whalefall, a $22.6M WW fifth weekend (3rd place) to awful $17.5M global bow (6th place)  	The second big screen take of a Capcom game in the market, Resident Evil, saw $17.1M (-36%) from overseas at 67 markets and 31K screens with $5.5M domestic. Running global cume is $361.1M ($212.7M of that from foreign). Top-performing markets by cume are China $56.0M, UK $18.2M, Mexico $12.4M, Australia $9.1M, Japan $8.5M, France $8.5M, Germany $8.2M, and Spain $7.7M. Constantin has Germany speaking territories with Metropolitan handling France and Sony the rest of the world.   	It was one of the best thrillers of 2023 on the New York Times list, which is why 20th made it. Some rival distribution sources believe that Disney would have best positioned Whalefall as a genre film so that it could over perform, however, they couldn’t alienate the book’s fans. While Whalefall on its net $60M production cost tanked with a No. 4 opening, somewhere in the world it was No. 1 and that was in Bosnia, Kuwait and Sauda Arabia ($400K). UK was high at $700K. The pic was No. 2 in China ($700K), Korea (wow, beating Street Fighter with $400K), Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Bahrain, Croatia, Iraq, Jordan, Lithuania, Oman, Qatar and UAE ($400K). The Brian Duffield directed movie was No. 3 in Japan ($500K) as well as Philippines Lebanon, Serbia, Slovenia and Ecuador. Disney says Whalefall opened within the top 5 US films in Mexico ($800K, best territory for the movie), Germany ($500K), Italy ($400K), Spain, and Brazil. France did $500K.  	Universal/Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s second weekend of Other Mommy was fourth with a $17.9M WW take ($9.5M int’l at 65 territories, $8.3M domestic, -70% on that D+ CinemaScore). Big running global cume at $78.7M ($33.9M foreign, $44.8M domestic) off that net $19M production price tag. That beats the reported cume of Jessica Chastain’s spooky movie Crimson Peak ($74.6M WW), but it still has a way to go if it’s going to overtake her Mama ($146.4M WW).   Other Mommy in France did $1.2M at 264 screens which included $118K previews. The standard opening was above Speak No Evil. Belgium bowed to $170K, No. 2 in the market behind The Odyssey, across 70 screens. An opening at this level is above The Black Phone and well above Black Phone 2. Holdovers included UK/Ireland with $1.2M in weekend 2 and a $5M cume, ahead of Black Phone. Italy delivered a second frame of $1M for a No. 2 behind a local title and a $3.7M cume, ahead of the lifetimes of Weapons and Evil Dead Rise. Mexico minted $900K with a $3.4M cume. Spain did $600K for a $2.3M running cume, ahead of Black Phone and Speak No Evil. Australia was $500K for $1.9M cume, in line with Black Phone 2.             	Fifth around the globe was Amazon MGM Studio’s third weekend of Colleen Hoover’s Verity with $17.6M WW ($11.4M int’l and $6.2M domestic). Worldwide stands at $145.3M ($79.2M offshore, $66.2M North America). The movie clicked past Regretting You ($90.4M WW) as Hoover’s second best around the world a while ago, and it will remain that way as It Ends With Us is such high bar at $351.4M WW.   	Dakota Johnson, Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett are still No. 1 in Germany with $1.9M (-27%) at 685 screens and a near $10M cume. Slovakia opened to $140K from 80 screens for a No. 1 rank, by far the biggest opening for a Hoover book adaptation there. Brazil still great with a No. 2 of $1.2M at 1,000 screens, -40% for a $9.1M cume. UK posted $1.5M at 657 screens, down -43% and a No. 3 rank for a running tally of $12.6M. By Nellie Andreeva  Editor-In-Chief  Jesse Eisenberg is shifting his attention to television. Coming off his latest movie as a writer-director, A24‘s The Debut, starring Julianne Moore, Eisenberg is prepping a TV series, also for A24. Written, executive produced and to be directed by Eisenberg, the show, which is expected to be taken out in the coming weeks, is executive produced by former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice, who was just named Chief Content Officer for Netflix, under his A24 deal.   	The yet-untitled series is based on a short story by Eisenberg about a young woman where new ideas and relationships challenge her beliefs, sources said. In a interview with THR on the red carpet for the London Film Festival premiere of The Debut, Eisenberg noted that It is about the beginning of the culture wars and follows an 18-year-old girl in the fall of 2002. Watch on Deadline		       	Netflix — now with Rice at the content helm — will likely be in the mix for the series; the streamer is home to such high-profile A24 shows as Beef and the upcoming untitled Millie Bobby Brown & David Harbour spy drama and Trigger Point, headlined by Joel Edgerton.   	Given Rice’s new job, he is not expected to have hands-on involvement going forward but will likely retain his executive producer credit having developed the series. Netflix’s top film executive Dan Lin and Ori Marmur remain EPs on Netflix’s Avatar: The Last Airbender series and Prime Video’s The Boys franchise, respectively.  	After an early stage career as a child actor, Eisenberg made his screen debut on TV as part of the main cast of Fox’s 1999 comedy-drama series Get Real. He then transitioned to movies where his main focus has been for the past two and a half decades, including his Oscar-nominated performance as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network and his Oscar win for writing his 2024 feature A Real Pain.             The Debut marks Eisenberg’s third feature as a writer-director, following the 2022 When You Finish Saving the World and A Real Pain. In TV, he most recently starred in the 2022 FX limited series Fleishman Is In Trouble. He previously developed a TV series adaptation of his short story collection Bream Gives Me Hiccups for Amazon and A24 a decade ago and single-camera comedy The Market for J.J. Login  Peter  18 October 2026   Deals Samsung Motorola Google Apple  Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days soaked up almost all of the discounts last week, so there wasn’t much left over for the weekend. This week, however, we are seeing a return to form. The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 starts at €1,405. This is for a 12/256GB unit and, unfortunately, the 512GB upgrade is still quite expensive at €425 more. Still, a nearly €600 discount on the base model is nothing to sneeze at. But is the new wide foldable form factor better than the book-style format? Our Galaxy Z Fold8 vs. Z Fold8 Ultra article goes into the pros and cons of each design. Speaking of, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra is quite expensive. A couple of weeks ago, it was €1,715 for a 12/512GB unit. Now, even the base 12/256GB unit is €1,830. If you decide you want the Z Fold8 Ultra, we’d advise you to wait. In the meantime, you can check out our Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra to help you pick which model is better suited for your needs. You should also consider some alternatives. The Motorola Razr Fold was €1,330 two weeks ago, now it’s €120 more. That’s still cheaper than the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, though. The Moto phone is thicker (10.1mm vs. 8.9mm) and heavier (243g vs. 215g), but it does have a larger battery (6,000mAh vs. 5,000mAh). It’s down on performance (Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 vs. the Elite Gen 5 chipset). However, the camera setup is competitive enough – 50MP 1/1.28” vs. 200MP 1/1.3” main, 50MP 3x/71mm vs. 10MP 3x/69mm telephoto and 50MP 122° vs. 50MP 120° ultra-wide. Both phones are slated for 7 OS updates (but note that the Galaxy launched with Android 17, while Motorola launched its foldable with Android 16). There’s also the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. However, the lack of big discounts makes it hard to recommend – as if the Tensor G6 alone wasn’t enough to disqualify it from the running. In contrast to the Ultra, the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 actually improved its price – the base 12/256GB model is €10 less than it was a couple of weeks ago and now a 12/512GB variant is available too with a similar discount. The vivo X500 Ultra is expected to launch in China in early 2027. Whether it will be available globally and when is still being decided. So, for now we have the vivo X300 Ultra. It has a token discount of €100 (which isn’t much, given its €2,000 MSRP) and it comes with a free 100W FlashCharge adapter. It’s not much in terms of freebies, but this is one of the best camera phones of 2026 and it is equipped with a generous 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. Check out our video review for a closer look at the phone. We’re skipping over the Galaxy S26 series this week. The Galaxy S26 Ultra (12/256GB) is available for €1,150, but considering that this same model was €960 two weeks ago, we’d advise you to wait. The Pixel 11 series, meanwhile, has more or less retained its prices from that time – for better or for worse. The Google Pixel 11 Pro XL is €1,280 for a 16/512GB unit, which is just €10 more than it cost two weeks ago. Either way, the €250 discount doesn’t look amazing compared to nearly €600 off on a cutting-edge foldable (the Z Fold8). The Pro XL is a larger version of the Pro, but it does have some advantages like faster charging and better speakers. The Google Pixel 11 Pro is available in both 12/256GB and 16/512GB configurations (note the different RAM capacities). These prices are within €20 of where they were two weeks ago. However, even with bad discounts, a Galaxy S26 (12/512GB) is €870. This model was €820 two weeks ago, so the price hike isn’t nearly as bad as for the S26 Ultra, but you can still do better. And the 12/256GB S26 configuration is out of stock. €820 can buy you a vanilla Pixel 11, by the way. It’s not as good as the Pixel 11 Pro, but being €150 cheaper than the equivalent Pro model makes the Pixel 11 worthy of consideration. Or you could wait for the S26 to drop to €820 again. Apple started accepting pre-orders for the iPhone Duo on Friday. Pre-orders are live in Germany, as well as Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, France, India, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Singapore, South Korea, Turkey, the UAE, the UK, the US and Vietnam. Shipments will start next week (October 23). That is only for those who can afford the massive price tag, of course – the base 256GB model is €2,300, which is nearly €900 more than the current price of the Z Fold8 (the Duo is a wide foldable). For context, here are the prices of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. They certainly aren’t cheap either, but unless you’re eager to try out Apple’s first attempt at a foldable, the standard iPhone models may be the better pick. Affordability continues to be a "real challenge" for some house buyers, after prices in Wales rose by 4% in the year to June. The market has shown "real resilience" with prices more than 7.5 times the average income in some areas, according to new figures from the Principality Building Society (PBS). Anglesey topped the chart with a 22% annual rise, but 17 of Wales' 22 local authority areas saw price increases, the Wales House Price Index said. Ceredigion was one of four regions to see a price drop and Aberystwyth estate agent Layla Mangan, said she has noticed "a lack of confidence" amongst buyers and sellers who were feeling "uncertain" about cost of living pressures. The overall average house price was Â£258,129, but Andy Mottram of PBS said, while the market had shown "real resilience" with "strong price growth" in many places, "affordability was a real challenge for people". Flintshire, saw no annual change and, of the four local authority areas to see a decline, Ceredigion had the the biggest drop of 9% - although Mangan said that did not reflect her experience in Aberystwyth. First-time buyers were facing average house prices equivalent to four-and-a-half times household income in Cardiff, compared with just over three-and-a-half times in Blaenau Gwent where houses were cheapest, according to the data. For people who were already home owners and wishing to move, purchase prices were equivalent to 7.6 times income in Cardiff and 5.2 times in Blaenau Gwent. Blaenau Gwent saw a 47% increase in the number of mortgages issued between April and June compared to the first three months of 2026, the biggest increase in Wales. First time buyer properties in the area cost an average of Â£155,000 with an overall house price of Â£167,239. But Blaenau Gwent also had the lowest average household pre-tax income at Â£42,000 according to the report. This contrasts with Monmouthshire which had the highest household income at Â£61,700 as well as the most expensive average house prices at Â£285,000 for a first-time buyer and Â£387,606 overall. Layla Mangan from Alexanders estate agent in Aberystwyth said she was "surprised" at the 9.3% drop in prices recorded for Ceredigion. "That's not been our experience" she said, "it's a hard market, yes, but it doesn't feel that we've dropped nearly 10%". Estate agent Layla Mangan says the Ceredigion housing market is reflecting uncertainty But Mangan said she has noticed "a lack of confidence" among buyers and sellers. "We don't have to look hard to work out why that would be. What an uncertain time we're in," she said. "I can understand people feel reluctant to wanting to essentially get into more debt. I understand that and it's hard at the moment." "Everybody is really into house prices, whether you're a homeowner or not, because we can use it as this kind of thermometer, this gauge for what the economy and our finances are doing in general," she said. "If you aren't looking at selling again in 12 months' time I'd hold your nerve, I'd go for it. "We can't expect to be buying houses and making money on them straight away and where we go wrong is if that's what we're expecting." The number of houses sold in a region can impact how much prices rise or fall compared to other places. On Anglesey, which saw the biggest annual rise in house prices of 22.2%, the market can be a mixed picture. Richard Tuke has lived on the island for 20 years but now wants to sell up and live in Spain. "Anglesey has always been a desirable area for people to live," he said, adding he thinks the market is "not as bad as it was". After several months of little interest he has twice reduced his asking price, from the initial Â£475,000 to Â£425,000, and that has made a difference. "We've had a wave of viewings in the last two weeks and a lot of strong interest, so I think we're at the right price level now," he said. The turbulence in the Middle East and the knock-on effects on oil and gas prices have already led to higher rates for fixed rate mortgage deals, and the Bank of England is widely expected to increase interest rates, making borrowing more expensive in the months ahead. "If you look back over the year to date, the market's shown remarkable resilience in spite of those pressures," said Mottram. "I think that's broadly likely to continue as we look forward." Mottram said that despite building cost of living pressures, there were a variety of options for would-be home buyers. "There's still going to be pressures," he said, but "if people are worried, the best thing they can do is talk to their lender or talk to a mortgage broker to understand their options". On Jan. 1, 2000, the world got a reprieve from a much-hyped technological Armageddon when it turned out the Y2K crisis wasn’t a crisis after all. Still, a real threat was looming if anyone paid attention to the stock market.  A new and life-changing business known as the internet, you will recall, was going to make us all rich, and not just the oligarchs behind the technology.  Dot-com stocks — even those of companies that weren’t making money, and that means most of them — were also supposed to defy common sense and gravity.  We were in a “new paradigm” — the code word for the era’s irrational exuberance in which emotion rather than metrics pushed stock valuations.  At the time, few people heeded warnings that not every business with that “new economy” suffix was destined for greatness.  It didn’t matter to masses of new investors who flooded the markets armed with the opinions of financial TV touts and newly invented discount brokerages as they kept buying with clicks on a computer screen. People with no real knowledge of Wall Street suddenly rivaled Warren Buffett for their acumen picking these no-lose stocks.  It was all the rage in financial media at the time, overwhelming the occasional Cassandras who just didn’t get it.  That is, until reality set in.  In March of that year, the historic stock run-up was exposed as one of history’s great investment bubbles. Many of the business models of the companies in the middle of the frenzy and the subsequent collapse were outright insane; most just overvalued by the market.  A precious few held real and tangible promise, but they too needed to survive the correction.  The losses were staggering.  A generation of investors were burned.  The tech market took years to recover from the fallout.  History, I’m afraid to say, does repeat itself when it comes to market manias.  That’s why our current mania involving all things AI will almost certainly follow the same trajectory with investor losses to follow.  Exactly what prompted the internet mood shift back in the day — and what will spark the coming artificial intelligence 180 — is hard to pinpoint. The most likely culprit: the collective instincts of the smart money of hedge funds and institutions that do their own research and filter out TV touts as opposed to the faux Buffetts who don’t.  As they did back during the dot-com mania, these investors are now sensing that something isn’t quite right with AI, the data and the Wall Street sales machine.  Then as now, big investors began to take profits and then more.  When the market crashed back in 2000 it was not just speculative stuff like promises of a Pets.com becoming the next Microsoft. The aforementioned tech giant got swept up in the mood shift as well, as did just about any public company that was tied to this revolutionary business.  Scary stuff for small investors who dived into the market and never looked back until they lost everything — and many did.  What’s even scarier is that most investors either don’t remember those crazy days or are blissfully ignorant of the past as they weigh what’s up with AI and want to be part of the hype.  The AI hype is so similar to the dot-com hype it’s almost breathtaking.  The sales pitch is nearly the same: groundbreaking stuff (which is true) that all investors, not just the oligarchs, will get rich from (which really isn’t). It may be true someday, though if history is any guide, that day is far off and getting there will be messy.  I can’t tell you whether last week’s market ructions — spiking rates after a bad inflation report then a selloff in AI stocks — is the herd making its final statement on AI by rearing its ugly head as it did back in 2000.  There might be more froth to come; IPOs by hyperscalers like Anthropic and possibly OpenAI could hit in the coming weeks and months.  But common sense and history teaches us it won’t last.  Interest rates will increase because AI is in competition with the massive borrowing needs of the federal government.  The correction is coming to AI and all the companies tapping into its technology through big spending, much of it using debt, the main ingredient of any crash.  If history is any guide, it’s time to take your profits and not get greedy — or pray that whichever AI you’re betting on will be a survivor of the crash that’s coming.

In recent weeks, I’ve been fortunate enough to observe two competing visions for Democratic senators should they retake the upper chamber in next month’s midterm elections. On the one hand, we have Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, who announced at the end of September that they were teaming up with their Republican counterparts Mike Lee and Shelley Moore Capito on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which the quartet believe will “reform the federal environmental review and permitting process.” Per their press release, “This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.” On the other hand, we have Senator Jon Ossoff, who has taken the debate stage twice in recent days to tell his Republican opponent to his face that he’s a racist scumbag. My paraphrasing here is more blunt than the rhetoric that Ossoff has been using, but only just. In the pair’s first debate, Ossoff threw daggers, accusing Representative Mike Collins of hiring “half the Third Reich to staff [his] congressional office,” adding, “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.” During Tuesday night’s debate, an embittered Collins tried to play the civility card, claiming that Ossoff’s incendiary statements about Collins’s very real embrace of white supremacy had led to death threats. Ossoff breezily brushed away the accusation and went back for more. Referring to Collins’s son-in-law, a white-nationalist influencer, Ossoff jabbed: “Can you commit for just three weeks to stop the production of neo-Nazi propaganda from your home?” This is like watching a fever finally break, and it’s not just Ossoff. In the Michigan Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed has gone at Mike Rogers with both barrels, repeatedly referring to the former congressman as weak and cowardly. In Maine … well, let’s just say that I wished Troy Jackson had a bit of that dog in him, but he doesn’t. Still, I can tell he’s trying, and his better moments against Senator Susan Collins, like telling her “You can’t eat road salt,” at least have a bit of a surly edge. At any rate, the rise of rude Democrats has got me believing in the potential cure for one of our greatest civic maladies: degenerative Senate brain, the very condition that leads a Sheldon Whitehouse or a Martin Heinrich to work with MAGA filth bent on desecrating the constitutional order. Right now, there should not be a bipartisan anything, unless it’s a negotiated agreement to mass-retire Republican lawmakers. As I’ve noted numerous times before, the GOP is essentially a criminal syndicate, aiding and backstopping a corrupt and self-dealing presidential administration. There can be no collaboration with Donald Trump and his goons on any level. So, no: I don’t want to see Democrats reaching for comity and accommodation. I don’t want collegiality. What I want to see is Democrats dogwalking their Republican opponents on live television. People like Ossoff are giving me faith that there are members of this party who are truly wedded to the notion of robust accountability, which is what the post-Trump era desperately needs. One thing that the years ahead can do without, however, is pundit and anthropomorphic smarm-fountain David Brooks, who is apparently not a fan of Ossoff’s sublime debating technique. This week, in an appearance on PBS Newshour, Brooks complained, “Jon Ossoff, my advice to him is, if you start calling your political opponents Nazis, maybe it’s time to shut up. That’s just not what we do here in this country.” Let’s take a look at the litany of things that we have been doing in this country that occasional TNR contributor Greg Greene compiled in response to Brooks’s call for toned-down rhetoric. The Trump administration is putting the finishing touches on a new prison for immigrant children and families. It has continued to murder people in the Caribbean. It has destroyed a girls’ school in Iran with a “double-tap” strike, killing 165 people. The shuttering of USAID has led to the needless deaths of hundreds of thousands of people. Just this week, Representative Ilhan Omar’s home was raided by federal agents in a trumped-up criminal probe into her citizenship. Then there’s the ICE violence, the criminalization of dissent, the abrogation of the media’s First Amendment rights, and the constant flow of white supremacist rhetoric from the Department of Homeland Security.  All of that is to say that, contrary to Brooks, I don’t think Ossoff’s debate rhetoric really rates as a problem right now. Let me put it plainly: Civility is a con. It’s a tool of the status quo. It’s most often called for when the people who get mauled by the powerful try to vindicate their rights or their humanity. It’s a brand wielded by smarmy phonies; demagoguery dressed in the robe of a high priest. And as TNR contributor Nacona Nix explained at length, the liberal commitment to civility theater does a lot of real-world harm: It’s currently one of the primary vectors by which antisocial and undemocratic ideas get laundered into respectability. And while it may seem laudatory to wish for a day when there’s nothing but an abundance of highmindedness for all to share, the Trump era can’t be ended by a change in tone or temperament. We can’t nice our way to a better future. As Nix writes, “The task now is not to lower the temperature, but to raise the standard.” Democrats should embrace the rudeness and vitriol if for no other reason than because it’s fully what the GOP deserves. But they should also just watch Ossoff cook, because the man is straight-up running a debate clinic. He’s calm, composed, and fully committed to tearing his Republican opponent to shreds. I find it comforting to watch Collins disconsolately shuffling his papers and stumbling back to his talking points. That he looks like a hunted man on that stage alongside Ossoff makes my soul feel lighter. That’s how Trump’s enablers should feel. That should be an essential part of the midterm message: Hunting season is coming. When I hear Ossoff’s debate rhetoric, I hear nothing discordant. I hear the sound of standards being raised. With the midterm elections less than a month away, it would seem to be an absurd time to suffer a thought for the next election cycle and the challenges that any would-be Democratic presidential victor would have to tend to on day one. Unfortunately, sometimes current events intercede with a potent reminder of just how rough the road to recovery and post-Trump renewal will be. One such story broke this week in the pages of The New York Times, which detailed some of the Trumpian luminaries who have recently ascended to important positions at the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, run by Trump acolyte Harmeet Dhillon.  The piece wastes no time: In short order, we’re introduced to “a former prosecutor forced off a high-profile murder case for peeking at the defense team’s strategy documents,” a “onetime gambling executive” with a sideline in promulgating “conspiracy theories about the Las Vegas massacre in 2017,” and a “Florida activist” whose “activism” included being jailed for several weeks for “hacking a local election system.” The long and the short of it is that the agency, once stocked with skilled professionals, is now chock-full of people who ordinarily wouldn’t pass the smell test for public service. Somewhere, a pool is missing its cess, and they might want to check whether it ended up at the DOJ. Much has been made of the way the Trump administration, returning to power with Project 2025 as its guiding manifesto and Elon Musk as its chainsaw-wielder, went to war with the civil service in the hopes that it could be ground down by purging the dedicated civil servants who’d previously staffed whatever posts were relevant in keeping us free of cyclospora. This Times story is covering the other side of the equation: The full Trumpian takeover isn’t just about firing people en masse. Frankly, it’s not merely about placing people loyal to the cause in top positions. It’s about stationing borderline lycanthropes in powerful positions. Daniel Flickinger, who began working on the division’s education cases earlier this year, was forced out of his job at a Birmingham, Alabama, law firm in 2020 after suggesting—to the disgust of his bosses—that George Floyd was fortunate to have died in a “fentanyl- and methamphetamine-numbed strangulation” because “it meant being worshiped in a nationwide funeral.” Peter Feaman, a veteran lawyer from Florida hired in early 2025 as a senior counsel, has a history of far-right political statements. In a May 2021 post on social media, he accused the “diabolical” Democratic governor of Michigan, Gretchen Whitmer, of forcing citizens into getting the “mark of the beast” (a coronavirus shot). This isn’t going to be a temporary problem by any means. The idea that the Trumpers who’ve come to Washington might take their leave if and when the federal government comes under Democratic control is a hopeful notion, but I worry that some of the true believers aren’t just here visiting; they intend to stay. That’s certainly the sense that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—who’s gone to great lengths to stuff the agency under his control with all manner of cranks and quacks—strove to convey at last week’s MAHA Summit in Washington, D.C. As Mother Jones reported, Kennedy “proclaimed the changes he’s wrought to HHS are permanent, and praised his allies in the movement for helping to make them happen.” “Even if I got hit by a truck tonight,” he bragged, “HHS will never go back to what it was before.” When it comes to government agencies that have suffered the most from this Trumpian takeover, none are as complete or as concerning as the Department of Homeland Security. On its best days, DHS is a walled garden of cops all hotboxing themselves with reactionary politics. Under Trump, it’s essentially become a hive of outlandish herrenvolk propaganda, pumping neo-Nazi memes into the social media bloodstream—the better to recruit the sort of person who might want to inflict terror on the streets of American cities.  As The New Republic’s Melissa Gira Grant documented, DHS’s tainted origin as a post-9/11 agency with a monomaniacal focus on Muslim extremism—and with a storied history of downplaying the threats of white nationalism—has only grown even more corrupted by the second coming of Trump. “We are doubling back around the same circular path,” Grant observed, “where agencies such as DHS downplay white nationalist violence, both potential and actual, while they draw recruits from those same ranks.” For a future Democratic president, the challenge of righting the ship of state will not simply be a matter of reviving the federal workforce and bringing competent professionals back to the perches they once occupied. It will be a matter of fumigation, as well—or, to use a better term, lustration, which Yale Law professor Dina Francesca Haynes, writing immediately after the first Trump administration, defined as “the process of vetting and removing from public service those who engage in or support extremism or seek to undermine democracy.” Lustration, Haynes explained, “has been carried out or proposed in many countries attempting to pull themselves from the wreckage of fascism, genocide, and nationalism.” As Haynes described, the idea is that for a country to successfully “move forward” from its authoritarian past, “it must rid itself of corrupt public servants by vetting them, and potentially dismissing from employment and cancelling pensions of those who harbor such deep bias that it would be impossible for them to fairly and impartially exercise the discretion they have been granted by virtue of their position in public service.” This is something that those of us at The New Republic have already begun considering as a necessary bridge back to a functioning democracy. In fact, as The New Republic’s Matt Ford pointed out as he gamed out what a future president could do to gut ICE, Trump himself has already provided the working blueprint for a quick and effective purge of any Trumpian fifth column that might remain gummed in the gears of government after the president leaves office. A future president can claim the same “vast powers to decide the fate of federal agencies,” including terminating employees, cutting funding, and transferring staff and programs to other agencies.  Elsewhere, Ford also suggested that a future Democratic president make use of the power Trump claimed for himself to “reduce headcounts through a reduction in force, perhaps by firing every agent hired since 2024.” As Ford opined at the time, the administration’s “decision to drastically reduce hiring standards for incoming ICE agents would more than justify such a sweeping action.” That the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division is studded with people who shouldn’t be managing a Pizza Hut, let alone prosecuting civil rights offenders, suggests there is ample room to expand these principles of lustration throughout a Trump-tainted civil service. As I’ve said before, the right way to think about the Trump administration and its wholesale operations across the federal government is to accept the fact that it is essentially a criminal syndicate, dedicated to self-enrichment and political corruption. The next Democratic administration should have accountability on its mind, and a commitment to rooting out the Trumpian rot that’s infected the civic architecture of this great nation. It might be that the most useful thing the Trump administration has accomplished in its odious lifetime is to provide the playbook to right its wrongs and dismantle Trumpism permanently. This week, one of the most talked-about stories has been President Donald Trump’s decision to spend taxpayer money on campaign ads that the administration is misleadingly characterizing as “public service announcements.” The move is vintage Trump in that the ads are both staggeringly corrupt—the administration is spending $20 million of the Department of Homeland Security’s money on them, in violation of the Hatch Act—and propagandizing slop. One ad, which uses a song without the artist’s permission, has Trump asking people, “Love me.” Another warns of a “final battle.” So far, the administration has only spent a fraction of the money that’s been allocated to this endeavor, so you can count on seeing many more iterations of these fake PSAs, which Trump is said to be guiding. But rather than think of this as some kind of flex, or one more scandalous abuse of the public trust, I want to suggest that what these ads represent is desperation—an acknowledgment that if Trump’s goose isn’t cooked yet, the pot is at least boiling. I also think, if anything, this fusillade of propaganda will likely backfire. These ads haven’t generated good news for Trump; very few people outside of the administration and its obvious sycophants have tried to defend them. Moreover, the media seems resistant to give this story the “both sides” treatment. As with Trump’s 25-minute prime-time ramble last July, the political press seems wise to what’s going on. Of that aforementioned speech, TNR editor Michael Tomasky said, the overall reaction to the president’s attempt to shine us on “tells us that that power he had over people and institutions a year or 15 months ago has evanesced.” I think these PSAs do little else than advertise that fact. I am not sure that Republican lawmakers necessarily agree with that assessment, but their own appraisals range from avoidant to withering. As MS NOW reported this week, “even congressional Republicans are expressing concern that the ads may violate the laws governing PSAs.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune is quoted in the piece as saying that he didn’t mind the message of the ad but believed “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars.” That’s about the nicest thing any Republican who made their way into the story had to say about it, with Senator Mike Rounds saying, “It’s not something I would have done” and the outgoing Thom Tillis comparing it to Viktor Orbán. “I hate it,” said Tillis, bluntly.  Trump’s midterm activities aren’t limited to these controversial ads. According to reports, the president is planning to spend 32 of the next 35 days on the road campaigning for Republicans. As Politico notes, many of his intended destinations suggest the GOP is in tremendous peril. Instead of swing states and traditionally competitive districts, Trump is visiting “bastions of conservatism” like Alabama, Oklahoma, Ohio, and Texas. He’s even going to trek out to Alaska, “a significant commitment of time and presidential resources that underscores how dire the situation is for Republicans.” As one GOP donor told Politico, “The problem is that the fires are everywhere right now.” The biggest question is whether Trump’s growing effort to further inject himself into the midterm cycle is going to help or hinder the electoral hopes of Republican lawmakers. In at least one contentious race, the Republican candidate is calling Trump an albatross. According to leaked audio obtained by The New York Times, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton told a room full of donors that Trump’s weird midterm convention in early September—which was held in Texas, in the hopes it would boost Paxton—had the opposite effect. “So to be honest with you, the numbers—when we did that convention—it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.” (As Lawfare editor Eric Columbus pointed out, it’s also not good “when your 12-person private fundraiser includes someone who hates you enough to leak damaging audio.”)  The Paxton audio is a potent snapshot of some larger trends. All across the country, we’re seeing stories of GOP strongholds edging toward collapse as onetime Trump voters bear the weight of his administration’s incompetence. There are daily reminders that other Republicans are trying to create distance between the president and their campaigns, and even defying him on key matters. On Wednesday, in fact, West Virginia Senator Jim Justice broke with Trump on the matter dearest to the president’s heart—his mass deportation machine. “Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,” he said. You think? Over the course of the year, as Trump’s approvals hit new lows and began to decimate the GOP’s midterm ambitions, I’ve tried to figure out what Trump and his fellow Republicans could do to reverse or even just arrest those trends. For a brief mad moment, I thought that the negotiated Memorandum of Understanding between the U.S. and Iran might provide a springboard Trump could use to extricate himself from his crazy war. This didn’t come to fruition. The truth is, to save their bacon, Republicans would have to do things they are genetically incapable of doing: improve people’s lives and fix the economy. As I pointed out two weeks ago, Republicans—despite their misgivings about Trump—are still touting their One Big Beautiful Bill Act: a document that says the wealthiest among us deserve thousands of extra dollars, and the rest of us deserve some measure of pain. It’s all adding up to defeat. The Cook Political Report says a Democratic takeover of the House is a “done deal” and that winning the Senate is “very realistic.” The Quinnipiac generic poll of the House has Democrats opening up a 51 percent to 39 percent lead, which are bloodbath numbers. The only headwind Democrats face is that while voters seem willing to give them their vote this year, they’re not as ready to give them their affection. Still, you’d rather be the Democrats right now than the GOP, who like Vice President JD Vance have been left begging voters for a “second chance” without understanding that they’ve already received that second chance—and they’ve blown it.
