One of my many cataloged memories of the Trump era is from the run-up to the 2016 election, when one of my colleagues related to me what one of his sources in Brazil, fretful about Donald Trump’s rise, told him. “It’s OK for the world for Brazil to occasionally be a basket case nation,” he said. “But the thought of the U.S. becoming one is really disturbing.” This week, Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly, cast in the role we once reserved for people like Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and Muammar Qaddafi: the batshit egomaniac dictator (only this time, with nukes). It seems to me that we’ve well and truly failed the basket case test. But a new poll has given me some fresh worries on this front—and a concern that maybe too many of us have developed a little taste for misrule. The survey was published this week by Liberal Currents and it sought to catch the mood of the Democratic electorate as Election Day looms. Much of what the poll found was downright anodyne: A plurality of respondents favor Kamala Harris as the presidential nominee in 2028; “economy, inflation & cost of living” wins as the respondents’ biggest issue they want a future Democratic president to tackle. But one result made me do a double take. Under the section, “Feelings about Trump leaving office,” respondents were asked, “If you woke up tomorrow morning and saw the following news headlines, how would you feel?” One of the choices, “To ‘safeguard the Constitution,’ a group of U.S. military leaders have removed President Donald Trump from power and assumed control of the United States” earned a net approval of 31 percent, with 59 percent approving and 28 percent saying no. That’s not good! Now the reason I’m not completely disassociating is because the ways respondents answered the other choices were more rational: Impeachment was by far the favored choice of removing the president, at 80 percent net sentiment, followed by removal via the Twenty-Fifth Amendment at 77 percent, and “dying peacefully in his sleep” at 40 percent. Assassination—by far the most immoral and dangerous way Trump could leave office, for all the reasons I lay out here—was the only choice with a negative sentiment, as it should have. Still, I’m sorry, but the approval number for a military junta taking over the United States is way, way too high. Folks, you do not want a military coup in the United States under any circumstances. Perhaps one reason this idea polls so well is that we’ve recently had a sample taste of what it’s like to be under unconstitutional leadership and it led to a desirable outcome. During the January 6, 2021, insurrection and for about a fortnight after, the United States was for all intents and purposes governed by a weird triumvirate: Nancy Pelosi, Mike Pence, and General Mark A. Milley. Trump was, during this time, meaningfully constrained from exercising some of his constitutional authority, while this troika took it up. It can be argued, of course, that this may have been for the best. This interregnum eventually yielded to the Biden administration and its comparative normalcy. But for many people, myself included, it was still fairly unsettling. In many places around the world, such takeovers end badly.  This is perhaps why the basket case anecdote came flooding back in my memory banks, as Brazil’s history is demonstrative of why military coups d’état are a bad idea. If the Latin American nation is any guide, once you start having military takeovers, you tend to keep having them. As the Berlin Journal’s James N. Green recalls, “Since 1889, when the Brazilian army ousted Emperor Pedro II and established a republic, the armed forces initiated nine attempted takeovers, five of which were successful.” Brazilian history also teaches us that military takeovers can be very difficult to dislodge. “The last military intervention into Brazilian politics took place in 1964, with the explicit support of the U.S. government,” writes Green. “It led to a 21-year-long military dictatorship.” I feel it should be obvious to most that a Trump-ousting coup would be an incredibly combustible event that would shatter the political landscape and lead to widespread uproar that would be difficult to contain. As I’ve noted previously, the MAGA movement is steeped in conspiratorial thinking and bound in cultlike devotion to Trump. Martyring him is thus a very bad idea. A military-style coup d’état would likely reinflame the passions that led to the January 6 insurrection, and serve as rocket fuel for the growing number of people who TNR’s Matt Ford says claim “a purported Second Amendment right to murder civil servants and assassinate elected officials.” As TNR’s Tim Noah wrote earlier this week, one Trump-removal scenario that’s on the table comes down to the GOP’s long-term political thinking: Should Republicans get battered in the midterm elections, there could be a strong incentive to convince Trump to retire or quit and pass the torch early to Vice President JD Vance, so as to allow him two years to essentially run as an incumbent. If that’s the way it goes, so be it. Trump would, of course, have strong incentives to stay, as his becoming a private citizen again would immediately embroil him anew in any number of legal battles. Barring that, the constitutional methods of removal that most Democrats thankfully seem to favor are the better options—though it seems that impeachment is, for Democratic leadership anyway, off the table. Perhaps it would be impractical for a newly empowered Democratic Congress to try impeachment for a third time (though they say that’s “the charm”). Still, it’s worth remembering that Republican senators had two shots to end a derelict presidency—once immediately after he sicced a mob on them—and they failed in their duty to oust Trump and bar him from holding public office. In this way, impeachment should remain a salient issue in this autumn’s Senate races: All of the miseries we are experiencing right now would never have happened if enough Republican senators truly loved their country. It needs to be said that if Trump’s reign is to end prematurely—that is, before his stepping down on the next Inauguration Day—things won’t be peaches and cream. Even if it comes about through constitutional means, the U.S. will have to navigate a period of tumult. If we’re contemplating the end of the Trump presidency, rather than indulge in fantasies about a military coup, we should all contemplate how each of us, in our own way, might help reinforce the civic foundation and serve as good stewards of a nation of laws. Perhaps, as Noah writes, we’re within sight of Trump’s fall. We should not take such matters lightly, because if the fall is all that’s left, it matters a great deal. Last week, President Donald Trump announced that if Republicans prevail in this year’s midterm elections, he would provide everybody with a $5,000 dividend check. People reacted as if he’d said something crazy, like “Barack Obama was born in Kenya and is ineligible to be president of the United States”—by which I mean they dismissed his ravings as one more Trumpian oddity and not what it really was: the disqualifying lunacy of a corrupt jackass. A few brave souls gently raised concerns that this was tantamount to a bribe. Those who wanted to add something substantive to the conversation pointed out just how much this idea would cause inflation to spike. I don’t recall anyone saying the obvious thing: A $5,000 payoff would be an implicit admission that he and his party’s reckless policies wrecked the economy and spawned a nationwide affordability crisis. House Speaker Mike Johnson, whose flock of lawmakers would ostensibly be the people who would find this money—more than $1 trillion—and appropriate it, told Kristen Welker in an interview that the so-called “Trump dividend” would be something lawmakers would “process through Congress and talk through and debate and discuss.” That said, nothing is happening anytime soon, because Johnson is sending lawmakers home until the midterm elections so as to avoid having to vote on GOP Representative Thomas Massie’s proposed impeachment of Secretary of “War” Pete Hegseth, who, between psychosexual panic attacks about the masculinity of the soldiers in his presence, is currently getting the belt-to-ass treatment from Iran. So you might have to wait a while for your $5,000 check. But that doesn’t mean that the Trump dividend hasn’t already been paid out. To the contrary, the president and his congressional enablers have been handing out money left and right. They’ve made people very rich, in fact. It’s something that they’re quite good at doing—at least for a few. Once upon a time, Trump claimed that shared prosperity would come in the form of tariffs, which he believed would rake in such a large amount of revenue that the income tax could be abolished. This was insane in theory; in practice, Trump’s tariffs only followed the logic of the president’s ire—whatever nation was pissing him off that week would get tariffed. The Supreme Court eventually ruled that most of this nonsense was illegal, not that it diminished Trump’s yen for trade war. But it’s not all bad news. As ABC News reported last month, the administration has paid out $100 billion in tariff refunds. That ought to excite everyone. After all, the Tax Foundation estimates that the tariffs that the Supreme Court ruled to be illegal cost every household $700, so a reimbursement might be helpful in filling up your gas tank three or four times. But as ABC News notes, “most consumers—who paid higher prices from the tariffs—aren’t seeing that money go back into their pockets.” In some instances, firms have plans to repay some of that money to consumers. But in other cases, that money is being pocketed, with some corporations earmarking the money for “reinvestment” and others putting it toward offsetting the other high costs they face because of Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war.  And for small businesses, these mini windfalls have arrived too late. Per ABC, one fortunate recipient of a $50,000 refund says “she was forced to cut staff and use her retirement savings to keep the business afloat” while waiting for her refund pittance. That’s wreckage the check won’t cover. All in all, Trump’s “Liberation Day” mainly liberated money from your pocket. Whether it makes its way back to you or remains in the coffers of corporations is anyone’s guess. Meanwhile, people seem to be forgetting that Republicans in Congress have already passed a measure that put $5,000 in Americans’ pockets—or to be more precise, $5,190 to Americans earning between $153,600 and $361,400. That law is called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has been one big beautiful means of cementing income inequality across the country. As the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy reports, the OBBBA “favors the richest taxpayers and provides working-class Americans with relatively small tax cuts that will in many cases be more than offset by the import taxes, or tariffs, imposed by President Trump.” The richest 1 percent got way more than five grand in this deal—their tax savings were in excess of $66,000. At the other end of the spectrum, the poorest 20 percent got a paltry 40 bucks. Don’t spend it all in one place! (Actually, many folks cannot because the same bill ended the Affordable Care Act subsidies they were using to purchase health insurance.) Republicans’ monomaniacal focus on re-enriching the already rich is doing much more than thieving money from your pocket. Wealth concentration is increasingly locking most of us out of the American dream. As a 2024 study from the Institute for Policy Studies and Popular Democracy found, wealth concentration is “supercharging existing problems of gentrification, homelessness, unaffordable rental housing, and out-of-reach homeownership.” Across the country, predatory billionaires are buying up single-family homes, keeping many of these properties vacant so as to “profit from real estate speculation,” and invading the short-term rental market to play the same tricks, thus keeping units at arm’s length from would-be renters. Trump and GOP lawmakers have enabled all of this through policies that have—as of Tax Day 2026—grown billionaire wealth 30.6 percent. If you’re like most people, you could use $5,000 right about now. As a recent memo from Americans for Tax Fairness noted, “Working Americans have had to pay more for health care, gas, and food while their paychecks have remained stagnant or fallen while [Trump has] been in office.” Meanwhile, as Republicans wiggle and dodge on the Trump dividend checks, they’re out in public touting the very bill that led to all of this widespread immiseration—and hiding the fact that when the Medicaid work requirements slated to be imposed after the midterms go into effect, an estimated seven million people won’t have health insurance anymore. Lots of people have gotten the Trump dividend: Trump himself, his family, billionaires, many corporations, even that weird Dick Tracy villain guy who broke the Reflecting Pool. But Trump’s long history of stiffing people should be more than enough to dissuade you from the belief that a check is coming your way if the GOP retains its majorities in Congress. If history is any guide, the Republicans would keep fleecing you. But the Trump dividends will continue to flow, and many people will keep getting richer. As they say, it’s a big club, and you’re not in it. This article first appeared in Power Mad, a weekly TNR newsletter authored by deputy editor Jason Linkins. Sign up here.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says. The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars. "You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says. He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune. We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction. Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.  Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs. We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States. At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over. It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl. The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added. When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce." Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me. They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat. At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma. They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty. One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life. As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid. "It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement. Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose". "In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers. Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so. "The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it." Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds. His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina. That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine. "The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements." And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois. I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity. Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means. He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever. When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico.  "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability." And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.   "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me. Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening. "In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel." The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures. Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens. It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters. "Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained. Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures. In August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search. As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of. As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates. The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper. Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected. Outside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them. In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell. Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs. She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing." Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants. The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous". "Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me. Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me.  And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics. "The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it." Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail.  "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way." Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track. It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb. As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed." A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail. When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours." She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs." Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics. Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them. The Amazon Kindle Oasis is back in stock for a limited time on the main Amazon.com website in the United States. The Graphite model with 8GB of storage is $115, the Oasis Graphite model with 32GB of storage is $145, and the Champagne Gold model with 32GB is $144. These prices are very good; considering the last time the 8GB model was in stock, it cost over $178.00. All Kindle Oasis models that are back in stock are used,  this means they are returned or a trade-in for a newer model. The Oasis remains one of Amazon’s most-regarded e-readers because it was the last to have physical page-turn buttons. The Kindle Oasis 3 features a 7-inch E Ink Carta HD capacitive touchscreen display with a resolution of 1680 x 1264 and 300 PPI. The screen is glass, and the body is high-grade aluminum. It has a front-lit display and is the first Kindle with a color temperature system. The front-lit display and color system can both be controlled by slider bars in the quick settings menu, or can automatically be adjusted based on the time of day via the ambient light sensor. It has 25 LED lights total, 12 white and 13 amber. Underneath the hood is a Freescale/NXP IMX7 dual-core 1 GHZ processor with 512 MB of RAM. The Oasis keeps the two manual page-turn buttons on the right side of the screen, and the settings menu lets you reverse the page turns, so up is down and down is up, which is ideal for manga. This is the only Kindle model that has physical page turn buttons. If you hold the e-reader in one hand while reading an ebook, you can disable the touchscreen; this is useful on public transit. If you love reading in the bathtub or at the beach, the Kindle Oasis 3 is waterproof. It is certified IPX8 to protect against immersion in up to two meters of freshwater, for up to 60 minutes. If your Kindle is splashed with water, wipe it off with a soft cloth and keep on reading. If your Kindle is immersed in water, remove its cover, make sure no cables are plugged into the device, and do not attempt to charge your Kindle until it is completely dry. If your Kindle is immersed in salt water, chlorinated water, soapy water, or liquids other than fresh water, make sure you rinse that liquid out of the device with fresh water such as cold tap water. Then dry your Kindle. Michael Kozlowski is the editor-in-chief at Good e-Reader and has written about audiobooks and e-readers for the past fifteen years. Newspapers and websites such as the CBC, CNET, Engadget, Huffington Post and the New York Times have picked up his articles. He Lives in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.

AP Photo Attention is turning to the Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct. 22, where policymakers will decide on interest rates following recent turmoil in the country’s fund market. Most economists expect the central bank to cut its policy rate by 100 basis points at this week’s meeting. Expectations for a rate cut have been reinforced by September inflation data, which came in below market forecasts. Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation rate stood at 29.73 percent in September, below market expectations of 30.3 percent, marking the first reading below 30 percent since November 2021. Consumer prices rose 1.84 percent month-on-month. At its Sept. 10 meeting, the central bank kept the policy rate, the one-week repo auction rate, unchanged at 37 percent. The bank also maintained the overnight lending rate and overnight borrowing rate at 40 percent and 35.5 percent, respectively. According to the central bank’s Survey of Market Participants published last week, respondents expect another average 100 basis-point rate cut at the December meeting, with the policy rate projected to fall to 35 percent. For the Jan. 21, 2027 meeting, respondents expect a further average 65 basis-point reduction, bringing the policy rate to 34.35 percent. The survey showed expectations for the policy rate to decline to 29.01 percent in 12 months, 27.93 percent by the end of next year and 22.39 percent in 24 months. In a research note, brokerage house Tacirler Yatırım said the decline in annual inflation as of September and signs of cooling domestic demand were likely to create room for interest-rate cuts in the final quarter of the year. The brokerage, however, said the scope for easing could narrow if the inflation outlook fails to improve as much as expected. Integral Yatırım said persistent near-term inflation expectations would be among the key factors determining the pace of monetary easing, while declining longer-term inflation forecasts supported expectations for rate cuts. “The pace of the expected easing will be determined by monthly inflation readings and the convergence of expectations,” Integral Yatırım said. According to analyst Zeynel Balcı, a rate cut this week could create a positive backdrop for both the stock market and the real economy. Balcı said negative market pricing had continued and noted that the decline in Borsa Istanbul, which began on Sept. 16 after problems emerged in the fund market, accelerated following a warning from MSCI. MSCI on Oct. 15 announced an immediate, indefinite freeze on certain index-related adjustments for Turkish equities stemming from index reviews or corporate events. Institutional investors will need to see credible and sustained enforcement against coordinated trading and disclosure standards that enable independent verification of the free float of Turkish securities, MSCI said. MSCI stated that if sufficient progress is not demonstrated by June 2027, it will consider additional measures, including a consultation on a potential reclassification of the MSCI Türkiye Indexes from Emerging Market to Frontier or Standalone Market status. “Emerging market status is an important matter of prestige for Borsa Istanbul,” Balcı said. “More importantly, being relegated to a lower category would not only limit new foreign investor inflows but also risk losing existing investors. Therefore, it is of great importance that the warning is taken seriously and the necessary steps are taken,” he added. Türkiye plans to complete legal changes to strengthen its fight against capital market crimes by the beginning of 2027, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek announced on Oct. 16. The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Şimşek said in a statement in a social media post.  Newly appointed Iranian Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi threatened on Oct. 18 to inflict “enormous damage” on the United States and its allies in the Middle East if Washington resumes its military campaign against the country. Türkiye’s carpet industry generated $2.017 billion in export revenue from shipments totaling 391.984 million square meters to 186 countries and free zones in the first nine months of 2026, according to data compiled from the Turkish Exporters Assembly (TİM). Following impressive midweek victories in European competition, Trabzonspor and Beşiktaş will bring revamped, star-studded rosters into a high-stakes Süper Lig clash on Oct. 19.

I've always been a massive nerd when it comes to coding. In fact, nine-year-old me somehow decided that sitting down and learning Python was a better use of my free time than doing literally anything a normal nine-year-old would do. While other kids were busy playing games, I was busy figuring out how to write my own (admittedly terrible) programs. My fascination with coding never really went away. If anything, the rise of AI coding assistants has only made it worse. Sure, these tools do mean I now spend less time actually writing code myself, and memorizing syntax is something I barely have to worry about anymore. However, they've also made coding a lot more exciting for me. I can focus on experimenting with all the ideas jumping through my head, building things I probably wouldn't have attempted otherwise, and seeing just how far I can push these tools. Instead of settling for one specific AI coding tool, though, I'm a huge fan of experimenting with all the different options out there. Through all this experimenting, I stumbled upon a tool that beats Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity at their own game.  There's a massive issue with the big names that dominate the coding agent market. As with every other category of AI tools, the competition to offer the most features has gotten a little out of hand. Every other update seems to bring a handful of new features, add additional layers of complexity, or introduce something else that most users probably won't even need. Though having more features certainly isn't a bad thing, and many would argue that getting more value out of an existing subscription is always appreciated, I'd argue that it does mean these tools are becoming increasingly bloated. Unfortunately, this isn't just limited to coding agents from the big AI companies, like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity. Cursor has a worthy free rival—and it's surprisingly good. Even free, open-source alternatives like OpenCode seem to be heading in the same direction. This brings me to Pi, which is an extremely underrated coding agent that competes with the likes of the tools I mentioned above, but takes a completely different approach to how a coding agent works. Developed by Mario Zechner, Pi is a free, open-source coding agent that puts simplicity and minimalism first. It's described as an "extensible agent harness that you can make your own." You can take it for a spin by installing it through npm, provided you have Node.js installed on your computer. All you need to do is open your terminal and run the following command: npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent Once it's installed, you can launch Pi by opening your terminal, navigating to the directory of your choice that you want Pi to work with, and running the pi command.  Similar to all the others, it works directly from your terminal and has all the agentic capabilities you'd expect from a modern coding assistant. It can read files, write and modify code, execute commands, and work through complex coding tasks on your behalf. What sets it apart, though, is that it manages to do all this with just four tools enabled by default: read, write, edit, and bash. As their names suggest, these tools allow Pi to read files, create new ones, modify existing code, and run terminal commands. That's essentially all it needs to function as a coding agent. Now, this doesn't mean Pi only supports four tools. It actually comes with several other built-in tools, including grep, find, and ls, which you can enable whenever you need them. The difference is that Pi doesn't force all these tools on you from the get-go. This means that your context window isn't unnecessarily cluttered with tool definitions you might never even use, leaving more room for the actual task at hand. One of Pi's biggest selling points is its extension system, which lets you add practically any functionality you feel is missing. Extensions are written in TypeScript and can introduce custom tools, commands, keyboard shortcuts, and even changes to Pi's terminal interface. You can also use them to modify how the agent behaves, interact with different model providers, or automate specific parts of your workflow. Essentially, with Pi, the onus is on you to build the coding agent you want. Rather than the developers deciding which features you need and shipping them with every update, Pi gives you the foundation and lets you take things from there. The best part is that you don't even need to know TypeScript to get started with extensions. Since Pi is a coding agent itself, you can simply describe the functionality you want and ask it to build an extension for you. Alternatively, you can install extensions and packages that other developers have already created. For example, Claude Code ships with a built-in Plan Mode that lets you explore a codebase and map out a task before making any changes. Pi doesn't enable an equivalent feature by default, but that doesn't mean you're stuck without one. You can simply ask Pi to build a Plan Mode extension for you, complete with a custom command, restrictions on modifying files, and even a progress tracker.  With Claude Code, you're limited to using Anthropic's own models. With Codex, you're limited to using OpenAI's own models. With Antigravity, you're primarily limited to Google's own models (though you get older models from other providers). Sure, there are ways to get around these restrictions, but these tools are generally designed with their respective companies' models in mind. Pi, on the other hand, doesn't tie you to any particular AI provider. You can choose from models offered by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Mistral, Groq, xAI, Cerebras, and several other providers. It also supports services like OpenRouter, which gives you access to models from multiple providers through a single API. If you'd rather avoid cloud-based models altogether, you can even connect Pi to locally hosted models using tools like Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, or vLLM, allowing you to run models on your own hardware without relying on a third-party API. Getting started is relatively straightforward, too. You can authenticate with a supported provider using the /login command or configure an API key. Once you've connected your providers, you can use the /model command to switch between models without having to leave Pi or start over with a completely different coding agent. This means you can choose which model makes the most sense for a particular task, whether that's a powerful reasoning model for a complex project or a cheaper, faster alternative for simpler coding tasks. You're not locked into one company's ecosystem, and you get to decide how much you're willing to spend!  Of course, giving users this much freedom comes with a few drawbacks. Unlike some of its competitors, Pi doesn't come with a built-in permission system that asks for your approval before executing potentially dangerous commands. By default, it operates with the permissions of the user account running it, meaning a poorly interpreted prompt could potentially modify or delete files you never intended it to touch. Fortunately, Pi's extension system comes to the rescue here, too. For example, there's a community-made extension called pi-permission-system that lets you configure rules for what Pi is and isn't allowed to do. You can set commands to execute automatically, require your approval, or block them entirely. You can also restrict access to sensitive files and directories, giving you more control over what your coding agent can touch. Still, it's worth remembering that an extension-based permission system isn't the same thing as running Pi in a properly isolated environment. If you're working with sensitive files or simply don't want to risk an AI agent messing with your system, running Pi inside a container or sandbox is the safer approach! The message cap is the least interesting reason to pay for Pro. All that to say, I'm not saying that Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, or even OpenCode are bad tools. Far from it. I've spent countless hours experimenting with all of them, and there's a reason I keep going back to them. Having a feature-packed coding agent isn't necessarily a bad thing, especially when those features genuinely make your life easier. But I do think there's something refreshing about Pi's approach, and the fact that you can experiment with different models and build the coding agent you want without having to wait for the developers to introduce new features. You get to decide exactly what your coding agent looks like, how it behaves, and what it's capable of! We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. Nine of the companies behind those stocks have formally said no. Broadcom, UnitedHealth Group and Verizon are among the nine US-listed companies that objected to having their shares tokenized on OKXICE. The joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange disclosed the objections in a public notice dated October 15, 2026. The pushback covers roughly 14% of the stocks OKXICE first planned to offer. The full list of objectors includes Cerebras Systems, AppLovin, Applied Digital, Rocket Lab, CoreWeave, Verizon, Applied Optoelectronics, Broadcom and UnitedHealth Group. The companies raised concerns about how token trading could affect their stock prices and liquidity. They also flagged potential investor confusion from tokenized versions of their equity trading on a venue they have no affiliation with. Under the SEC framework governing these products, an issuer objection within the designated window blocks that company’s shares from being tokenized on that specific venue. The legal backdrop is the SEC’s Innovation Exemption, issued on September 17, 2026. It allows tokenized stocks to trade without full exchange registration, as long as platforms follow specific guidelines. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. After a platform notifies issuers, companies get a 30 calendar-day period to object to tokenization of their shares. OKXICE’s stock token platform is not yet live. It faces a 30-day waiting period after notice goes out to issuers, which is the window these nine companies used. OKXICE itself is a 50-50 joint venture between OKX and ICE, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange. OKXICE intends to offer 24/7 permissioned trading of tokenized stocks through Uniswap v4, settled with stablecoins such as USDC and USDT. OKXICE plans to move ahead with dozens of other stock offerings, including tokenized versions of Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft. The SEC opened the door to tokenized stocks, but it handed issuers a veto over individual venues. That turns every new listing batch into a negotiation, or at least a waiting game. A roughly 14% objection rate on a first batch suggests future offerings may never fully match a broad equity index. Most of the 63 companies on OKXICE’s initial list did not object within the window. The next markers to watch are OKXICE’s launch timing once its waiting period clears, which names make the final listing, and whether other tokenization platforms see similar objection rates when they send their own notices. The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market. A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy. The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations. It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels. There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey. Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures. "Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia. "Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help. "I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union." The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%. The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years". "Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine  Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer. But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment. All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently". At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added. Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began. Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids. "The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks." "Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged." Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history". "We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive." Watch CBS News  October 18, 2026 / 10:12 AM EDT             / CBS News            In most of the country, autumn is campaign season. But in Michigan it is also cider season. The Franklin Cider Mill is an institution in suburban Detroit that churns out hot donuts and ice-cold cider slushies. Between bites, we asked visitors to assess the state of their wallets three weeks before Election Day. "I would say most are struggling, if I'm being honest," one woman said. Another man offered, "I don't feel great about the economy right now." Jeffrey Robinson, a high school principal, put it succinctly: "It sucks," he said. "We have parents that carpool that are finding it hard to keep gas in the car." If it seems like people are feeling especially gloomy about the economy, Joanne Hsu has the proof. She runs the nation's longest-running consumer sentiment survey at the University of Michigan. It dates back to 1946. She says that, since the start of the Iran conflict, "We've been seeing quite a bit of decline in consumer sentiment across the board, across all walks of life." In fact, Hsu says, consumer sentiment is lower than almost any other time in modern history – including the stagflation era in the mid-1970s; the financial crisis in 2008; and the post-COVID price spikes under the Biden administration.   "Democrats, Independents and Republicans, all three groups, feel worse about the economy in this administration than they did in the first Trump administration," said Hsu.  And, she said, people are feeling bad about the economy despite the stock market doing well and rising wages. "The wages not keeping up with inflation is the key point there," Hsu said. "So, people don't feel like they're able to get ahead. The share of consumers who are expecting their wages to grow faster than inflation fell from 18% just a year-and-a-half ago, to only 11% in September. That's a huge drop." Hsu says consumer sentiment initially went up when Mr. Trump was reelected two years ago. But the president has failed to deliver on one of his key campaign promises, one he made right here in Michigan just a few weeks before Election Day. "One of my top priorities will be to quickly defeat inflation and make America affordable again," Mr. Trump said in 2024. "It'll all happen very quickly. This will rapidly drive prices down, lower interest rates, and put more money into the pockets of American consumers. It'll also bring your grocery bill way down." Instead, grocery prices rose by more than four percent in the past two years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics; gas prices are up 35 percent, according to AAA; and 30-year fixed mortgage rates are projected to stay above seven percent through next year, according to Freddie Mac. Real estate agent Michael Perna told us, "It would not surprise me if we saw a rate that starts with an 8 before we see a rate that starts with a 6." In Northville, Mich., a house that normally would have been on the market for just a week has been for sale for more than a month. Perna says the house is priced a little over what buyers can afford right now: "Originally the mortgage rates were about 6.5 percent, and now they're at 7.5 percent, and buyers can afford $50,000 less, [so] we're a little over." He says, even for homebuyers with a stable income, every rate hike means they have to settle for less – which makes for a pretty bad attitude about this economy. "Absolutely, a lot of people, myself included, have a bad attitude about this economy!" Perna said.  So, will sour consumers make for angry voters? Back at the Franklin Cider Mill, some are optimistic, but not all. One woman criticized President Trump's tariffs ("It raises all of our prices, so it's hard"), but thinks in the long term they are needed to bring more manufacturing jobs to the U.S. One man said this economy is not what he expected under Mr. Trump in his second term: "He promised us, and I don't think he kept his promise." High school principal Jeffrey Robinson said, "The average public is paying a price. I'm not looking for my $5,000 check, because I know that's not coming. But I don't know how long the economy and the average person is going to be able to sustain what we're going through right now."      Story produced by Mark Hudspeth. Latvia could allow residents to pay personal taxes with cryptocurrency as early as next year, as part of a push to attract crypto firms and investors. The country’s Finance Ministry has agreed to the plan, though technical work with a payment provider remains, said Didzis Dejus, an adviser to the prime minister on strategic planning and the new economy.  Asked whether Latvians would be able to pay taxes in crypto during the prime minister’s term, Dejus told CoinDesk at the UN:BLOCK Fintech conference in Riga that “I believe that will take place next year.” CoinDesk has reached out to Latvia’s Finance Ministry for comment but hasn’t heard back at the time of writing. The move would give crypto holders a way to use their assets to meet tax bills. It also builds on plans announced in May 2025 to enable crypto tax payments and the tokenization of other assets like real estate. “We are not afraid to be the fastest country,” Dejus said, describing efforts to attract crypto business beyond licensing. The proposal comes as Latvia changes how it taxes crypto investments. On Oct. 15, the country’s parliament passed legislation to tax withdrawals from crypto investment accounts once they exceed the amount deposited, rather than taxing each trade. The law also introduces a one-time declaration process. Holders can settle past tax obligations by paying 10% of their declared assets’ market value at the end of 2026. Declarations can be filed from April 1 to May 31, 2027, with the tax due by July 23. Dejus said the measure would help people who bought crypto years ago but lack records to prove what they paid. The payment plan’s timing could depend on the next government. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List won the Oct. 3 parliamentary election, and is expected to be renominated, but still needs coalition partners. Latvia would not be the first government to accept crypto for taxes. Colorado started allowing crypto tax payments through PayPal in 2022, with funds converted into dollars. Dejus did not name Latvia’s payment provider or say which cryptocurrencies would qualify to pay taxes. Smugglers in the Negev desert are increasingly using drones and helium balloons to transport narcotics across the border into Jordanian territory. Save Share Amman, Jordan – Jordanians fear the country’s border with Israel is turning into a major drug-smuggling route amid a surge in high-tech operations by gangs using drones and helium-filled balloons. Organised networks active in southern Israel’s Negev Desert have links to groups in Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, operating along one of the most heavily surveilled borders in the world, with Jordanian authorities increasingly concerned about the implications this could have for the kingdom. This escalation coincides with changes in the regional drug trade, particularly after the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024. Elements in his regime were linked to the manufacturing and distribution of Captagon, an illegal amphetamine stimulant. Syria became a hub for the distribution of Captagon to the Gulf, with Jordan a transit point and market for the drug. The Royal Jordanian Air Force carried out periodic strikes on drug manufacturing and smuggling points inside Syria, highlighting the huge security concerns Jordan had about the trade. Since the collapse of the Assad government and the establishment of a new authority that views the Captagon trade as a national security issue, there has been a decrease in the drug trade from Syria into Jordan. Although Druze militias in the Syrian province of Suwayda allegedly linked to Israel have been accused of continuing the drug trade, Jordanian security forces are increasingly focused on the Jordan-Israel border. The use of quadcopter drones and balloons is reportedly among the new tactics used by gangs in Israel to smuggle hashish, crystal meth, and amphetamines into Jordan. Jordanian security forces are said to be increasingly unhappy with the scale of the drug smuggling operations and have accused the Israeli army of not taking the issue seriously. Initial data from Jordanian forces recorded 17 interception operations linked to drones during the first half of 2026 in Jordan’s southwestern border area with Israel. They also recorded 231 smuggling and infiltration attempts and downed 56 drones across various borders during the same period.  Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al Jazeera that Jordanian forces were continuing efforts to prevent drugs from being smuggled into the kingdom. But they are evidently facing more complex activities by drug dealers. “There is an increase in drug smuggling operations from Israel to Jordan using drones,” he said. “The number of seized drug cases during the current year reached 15,342 cases. Trafficking cases constituted about 28 percent of them, compared with 72 percent for usage cases.” Israeli media reports indicate that gangs active in the Negev Desert are behind some of the smuggling operations into Jordan, where drugs can fetch higher profits. There are estimates that 1kg of hashish can sell for approximately 7,500 pounds sterling (almost $10,000), according to the British newspaper The Telegraph, which recently uncovered the drug smugglers’ latest operations. Israeli security services believe that the price of hashish in Jordan is about 15 times higher than in Israel. Due to widespread disenfranchisement and poverty, elements within Palestinian communities in Israel have been linked to the drug trade, according to reports. Multiple sources have accused Israel of allowing Palestinian towns and cities to become hotbeds of crime to create divisions and prevent calls for greater rights. Ammar al-Qudah, a member of the Jordanian Senate and retired major-general in the Public Security Directorate, claimed that organised gangs in the Negev had obtained more than 1,000 drones that were originally used for agricultural and security purposes. “The smuggling networks are linked to other gangs in Jordan, Sinai and the Negev, and rely on a route starting from Sinai, passing through the Negev, and reaching Wadi Araba, in addition to other routes including the Lebanese border with Israel and the Galilee region towards Syria,” he told Al Jazeera.      They are also using a range of sophisticated technology to bypass security on both sides of the border. This includes the use of helium-filled balloons equipped with GPS devices, drones capable of carrying about 50kg of narcotics, including black hashish and crystal meth, al-Qudah said. He warned that a portion of the black hashish and crystal meth being smuggled into the kingdom is being sold domestically, with the rest going to other markets in the region. With such high-tech operations, there are accusations that members of Israeli forces know about drug gang activities, based on past experiences in Egypt. One West Point report said current and former trackers in the Israeli military in the Negev are being recruited by traffickers to provide intelligence to facilitate their operations in Egypt. In 2012, a number of Israeli service personnel were arrested on suspicion of collaborating with drug smugglers across the Egyptian border. While there is no proof that the same situation is being repeated in Jordan, many have questioned how drones and balloons carrying drugs could cross a heavily surveilled and guarded Israeli border into Jordan. Jordan’s counternarcotics department, in cooperation with the armed forces, has tracked such cases and made arrests. Retired Brigadier-General Daifallah al-Daboubi, a strategic and military expert, said Jordan is witnessing a “reverse drug migration”, starting from the Sinai Peninsula, passing through the Negev region, and reaching the kingdom. “Groups active in Beersheba and the Negev possess great financial capabilities and use advanced smuggling methods, most notably drones,” he said. The Israeli army’s preoccupation with wars in Gaza, Lebanon and the occupied Golan Heights has provided smugglers with room to manoeuvre on the Jordan border, he added. But he ruled out the direct involvement of the Israeli political or military leadership in any drug smuggling. Steps taken by Israel to boost security on its eastern border include the establishment of the 96th Division, which began operating in the Jordan Valley in 2025, and the construction of a controversial security barrier with Jordan. But none of these measures appears to be designed to prevent drugs from leaving Israel; instead, they appear to be designed to prevent weapons and other illicit merchandise from entering the country from Jordan. IDC reported that memory costs have surged approximately 350% since last year and remain elevated, creating pressure on vendor margins and shipment volumes. The data center industry's demand for high-bandwidth memory has diverted manufacturing capacity away from consumer electronics, a dynamic reported earlier in 2026 as a critical shortage with implications for product roadmaps and component pricing [2]. The report's release came as analysts and market observers assessed the broader technology supply chain, where memory inflation has slowed to a low double-digit sequential increase in the third quarter, compared with growth of roughly 50% to 100% in prior quarters, IDC stated [1].Chinese Brands Face Pressure; Apple and Samsung Gain Share Chinese smartphone brands bore the heaviest impact from the cost surge, according to IDC vice president Francisco Jeronimo, who wrote in the report that corporate exposure to low-end handsets has forced vendors to choose between protecting margins and defending shipment volume as demand weakens [1]. Jeronimo described the quarter as showing "the full impact and damage of the memory crisis," and stated that higher shelf prices are prompting many buyers to keep their current devices longer [1]. The market shift has benefited Apple and Samsung, which IDC said are gaining market share through premium handset portfolios and supply advantages that help shield them from the downturn. The trend coincides with a shake-up in the premium segment: Huawei unveiled its Mate XT 2, a trifold smartphone that unfolds into a 10.2-inch tablet with a starting price of $2,980, a 10% increase over its predecessor, during Apple's launch week in September 2026 [3].Memory Chip Shortage Driven by AI Demand Raises Component Costs The downturn traces to an AI-related memory chip shortage that sent component costs soaring and forced manufacturers to raise handset prices beyond consumers' comfort zones, IDC said [1]. The shortage reflects data center demand for memory used in artificial intelligence workloads, which has competed with consumer electronics for constrained manufacturing capacity. A separate market monitor by Counterpoint Research reported that global smartphone shipments fell 11% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, reaching the lowest level in 13 years, driven by a persistent shortage of memory chips [4]. IDC wrote that memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in the third quarter compared with roughly 50% to 100% sequential growth in prior quarters, though costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch [1]. The pricing pressure has occurred alongside broader supply chain disruptions affecting electronics manufacturing, including prior episodes in which semiconductor factory fires and plant closures interrupted production of components used across the technology industry [5][6]. Observers of the supply chain have documented how shortages of a single component can cascade through production schedules and pricing for finished goods. The research literature on supply chain communication challenges notes that companies face persistent difficulties adjusting to new ways of communicating throughout supply chains when regulatory or market conditions change [7]. The current memory crisis has demonstrated similar dynamics, with a shortage in one category of components reshaping pricing and availability across the entire handset market.IDC Projects Shipment Pressure Through 2027; Recovery Not Before 2028 IDC expects handset shipment growth to remain under pressure through 2027, with any recovery pushed to 2028 at the earliest, according to the report. Manufacturers increasingly view the cost shock as a permanent change in the industry's economics rather than a temporary disruption. The forecast aligns with the assessment from Loop Capital's Donovan, who reported a 22% third-quarter decline and warned of "more pain to come," in line with IDC's findings [1]. The projected timeline suggests vendors will need to adapt to a higher-cost operating environment for multiple product cycles. Earlier reporting on memory shortages described how the scarcity of high-bandwidth memory and related components promised to reshape product roadmaps and corporate fortunes for years to come, with the price of computing projected to rise [2]. The industry's adjustment may extend beyond pricing into decisions about product portfolios, component sourcing, and geographic distribution of manufacturing. Financial markets have reflected concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout that has driven memory demand. Market commentary during the period described an AI unwind with technology stocks under pressure, as investors reassessed valuations tied to data center expansion and the semiconductor supply chain [8]. The volatility extended to semiconductor-adjacent markets, with analysts questioning whether current levels of AI investment can be sustained.Outlook Remains Negative as Vendors with Scale and Premium Mix Gain in Smaller Market Jeronimo said the pressure is now moving from vendors to consumers, as higher prices reach the shelf and volumes remain under pressure in coming quarters. Vendors with scale, secure supply, and a premium mix keep gaining share in a smaller market, according to the report [1]. The report's findings underscore a structural shift in an industry that had long benefited from falling component costs and expanding unit volumes. Manufacturers and consumers alike now confront a market in which memory and other critical components remain expensive, shaping purchasing decisions and product strategies well into the next decade.References   "Worst Is Yet To Come": Global Smartphone Shipments Crash 22% As Memory Crisis Squeezes Consumers. https://www.zerohedge.com/technology/worst-yet-come-global-smartphone-shipments-crash-22-memory-crisis-squeezes-consumers  NVIDIAs next gen GPU timeline UNRAVELS due to critical SHORTAGE price of computing projected to rise - NaturalNews.com, February 06, 2026. Week 7 is a good example of why college football is so special. Chaos. That was the theme of this weekend and it was great for viewing pleasure.  There were five teams ranked inside the top eight that suffered a loss on Saturday, and of course, upsets are always must-see TV. But it wasn’t just upsets that made Week 7 great.  Both of the must-see games went down to the wire. Despite losing starting quarterback Julian Sayin, Ohio State managed to stifle Indiana’s offense enough to get a big win on the road. And then Notre Dame-BYU didn’t disappoint. CJ Carr had a chance to get Notre Dame a big win, but the Cougars’ defense pulled out the upset to give the Irish their first loss.  Here’s the latest stock up, stock down from Week 7.  MORE: BYU makes No. 1 pitch: Notre Dame upset could end 42-year AP poll wait It was a big day for BYU and the Cougars wanted to show they belonged. The last time ESPN’s ‘College GameDay’ was in Provo was back in 2009 and that was a game BYU wants to forget. TCU crushed the Cougars, but it wasn’t going to be the same result this time around.  Despite not having running back LJ Martin, who has been BYU’s star, the Cougars got off to a quick start. BYU found itself up 21-10, but Notre Dame would make a run. The Irish would go up 24-21, and that’s when quarterback Bear Bachmeier showed his mettle. He led the Cougars down the field for a go-ahead score, and BYU would remain undefeated with a 28-24 win over the Irish.  BYU’s defense is for real and the Cougars are starting to separate themselves in the Big 12. Both Texas Tech and Utah will want to have a say, but BYU now has its signature win.  Three SEC teams ranked inside the top eight went down on Saturday. You can make the decision on whether the SEC is overrated or if there is just so much parity in the sport. It wasn’t that shocking to see Alabama lose. The Tide were up against a good Tennessee team on the road.  But Georgia losing a home game to Auburn? That wasn’t expected. Texas to lose a home game to Florida? A team that’s been reeling? Not expected. After seeing Alabama play Georgia last weekend, it appeared those were the best two teams in the SEC, but after this weekend, it could be Ole Miss, Tennessee, or Kentucky.  The days of Georgia, Alabama, and Texas dominating could be the thing of the past. With the new age of NIL and the transfer portal, the usual teams that dwell in the middle are making their way toward the top.  Tennessee is suddenly right in the mix of not only competing for an SEC title but earning a big bid in the College Football Playoff. The Volunteers are honestly a few plays away from beating Texas and being undefeated.  What makes the Tennessee win even sweeter for Volunteer fans is that they are doing it differently. We are used to seeing high-octane Tennessee teams, but with the Vols having quarterback issues, they rely on running back DeSean Bishop and their defense.  Bishop ran for 159 yards and two scores, while the Vols’ defense forced four takeaways en route to a 26-10 win over Alabama.  Texas has lost two games in a row, and two games in a row Arch Manning has had terrible moments. Last week, against Oklahoma, Manning had two fourth-quarter turnovers that cost the Longhorns the game against the Sooners.  This week, Manning struggled to take advantage of a susceptible Florida defense. And then in the fourth quarter, he fumbled the ball away. Manning had 173 yards through the air, and the Gators’ defense had allowed 270 or more passing yards in each of the last four games.  It’s time to have a talk about Manning and it’s because of his last name. Does he have major potential? Absolutely. But he’s yet to put it all together and there are little reasons to be talking about Manning has a top pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.  No Nico Iamaleava, no problem. The UCLA defense showed up last weekend against Oregon and it did so again this weekend against Wisconsin. The Bruins were just scoring more points than everyone else through the first four games, but now it’s up to the defense.  UCLA allowed Wisconsin to muster just 214 yards of offense in the Bruins’ 17-7 win over the Badgers. UCLA turned the ball over twice, but the Bruins’ defense wasn’t going to allow them to lose this game.  There are still concerns about UCLA. Ty Dieffenbach did throw for 264 yards, but he also tossed an interception and turnovers haunted him at Cal Poly last season. But if UCLA’s defense is going to take a new level, the Bruins have a schedule that will take them to the playoff.  Michigan was hopeful the bye week was going to fix its offensive woes. But that didn’t happen. In fact, the first 30 minutes against Penn State were among the worst football fans have witnessed. The Wolverines gained 80 total yards in the first half, and Bryce Underwood tossed two interceptions.  Kyle Whittingham benched Underwood in favor of freshman Tommy Carr to begin the second half. Carr led three scoring drives to propel Michigan to a 21-18 win over the Nittany Lions. by Benjamin Cottrell Pexels/Reddit Patience is always a rare commodity in a checkout line, but in this particular story, it was completely out of stock. One cashier, still new to retail, was doing her best to navigate a busy rush. A few items refused to scan, so a coworker stepped in to help while another register was called to open. The whole thing took maybe two or three minutes. But evidently that was too long for one entitled customer, who threw her pool noodles and towels on the floor, stormed out, and called the cashier horrible names on her way. A second register was opening right there, so she could have just walked over. Some people will do anything to avoid a short wait. Keep reading for the full story. I only recently started working in retail, which means I’m not as fast as a cashier as I was. Yesterday, it got fairly busy. We had a huge line, and I had trouble with some items not scanning. So the employees did their best to get by, but apparently their efforts weren’t enough for one exasperated customer. While one coworker was helping me figure everything out, we obviously called someone to open up another cash register. Apparently, we took too long, and this one lady in line just threw her shopping on the floor (some pool noodles and towels) and stormed out of the store, calling me horrible names while doing so. This employee was understandably flabbergasted by the brazen overreaction. And while I do get the frustration and how she probably had places to go, we really only took 2-3 minutes. Another cash register was opening that she could have gone to. This customer must have really been going through it. What did Reddit have to say? You never know how close someone is at any given moment to just completely snapping.  Many “adults” don’t act much like adults at all. Sign up to get our BEST stories of the week straight to your inbox.  If there’s one positive thing about working retail, it does help you build a pretty thick skin.  And another thing about this customer…  This customer turned a three-minute wait into a full-blown performance, and ironically, the only person who lost anything was her. The cashier was new, the scanner was being stubborn, and backup was already on the way, which is about as reasonable as a retail delay gets. Frustration is human, but a tantrum is a clear choice. Most Widely Read Newspaper Kindly share this story: The Lagos Commodities and Futures Exchange is targeting transparent petroleum pricing, stronger competition, and improved investment decisions by positioning organised commodities trading as a strategic instrument in Nigeria’s evolving downstream petroleum market. Following its recent licence from the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority to facilitate the trading and clearing of petroleum liquids, the Exchange is seeking to connect the physical petroleum market with Nigeria’s capital market through a structured, technology-enabled trading platform. The initiative comes amid significant changes in the petroleum industry, including downstream deregulation and expanding domestic refining capacity, which have heightened the need for reliable market information, transparent pricing, and efficient price discovery. In a statement by LCFE, its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Akin Akeredolu-Ale, said exchange-based trading will strengthen price discovery, competition, and investor confidence in Nigeria’s petroleum market.  He explained that the initiative would establish a credible marketplace where petroleum products could be traded through organised mechanisms supported by appropriate trading, clearing, and settlement processes, while attracting greater participation from refiners, petroleum marketers, traders, financial institutions, and investors.Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience.Add us to your Preferred Sources “At the heart of the initiative is the need to establish reliable domestic reference prices for petroleum products based on observable market activity rather than fragmented quotations and individual commercial negotiations. Price discovery is a fundamental function of a commodities exchange. By bringing buyers and sellers together within an organised marketplace, an exchange enables competing bids and offers to reveal the prices at which market participants are willing to transact,” Akeredolu-Ale said. He noted that the proposed framework would incorporate two-way quotations, standardised trading contracts, and transparent transaction processes to generate more dependable pricing information to help businesses evaluate supplier quotations, compare procurement costs, and assess prevailing market conditions. With increased participation and trading volumes, the Exchange could support the development of domestic reference prices that reflect Nigeria’s market realities, including local supply conditions, logistics, and other relevant pricing factors.         According to Akeredolu-Ale, the initiative could also reduce information asymmetry, which often makes it difficult for buyers and sellers to determine whether quoted prices are competitive or whether price differences reflect legitimate commercial considerations. “An organised exchange can help address this challenge by providing a common marketplace in which transactions and quotations can be assessed against more transparent market information. However, the development of a credible benchmark will depend on sustained trading activity, sufficient market liquidity, reliable transaction reporting and the participation of a broad range of buyers and sellers. The licensing milestone provides the regulatory foundation, but the depth and reliability of the eventual benchmark will depend on how effectively the market develops,” he said.
